documents.title: TM alert prioritisation reference data set documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1 used to develop, test and validate version 3.0 of model MDL-15 AML Transaction Monitoring, specifically its machine-learning alert prioritisation layer, and it follows the RDS documentation template of Annex A to MRM-STD-021. MDL-15 generates alerts on potentially unusual transactions of retail and business payment customers of the Bank through 18 rules-based detection scenarios and ranks those alerts with a gradient-boosted prioritisation model; the model is registered in the Model Inventory as a Tier 1 FEC model and is used to meet the Bank's transaction monitoring obligations under the Wwft and, from its date of application on 10 July 2027, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR). The scope of application comprises all natural persons, sole proprietors, small and medium-sized enterprises and corporate customers holding payment accounts with the Bank in the Netherlands; institutional and correspondent banking relationships are monitored by a separate model and are outside the scope of this RDS. The model is developed in-house by FEC Analytics; the scenario logic runs on a vendor rules engine (TMX platform, release 10.4) configured by the Bank, and the model is governed under MRM-POL-001 irrespective of the vendor component. The companion documents are the model development document EVD-15-MDD (TM scenario and tuning documentation), the data quality report EVD-15-DQ and the implementation and testing report EVD-15-IMPL.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: Chapter 2 describes the observation period of the alert-level RDS. The unit of observation is an alert generated by one of the TM scenarios in production and dispositioned by an analyst; the target is the investigation outcome of that alert as defined in chapter 3. All counts in chapters 2 to 6 are produced by the RDS build code at tag rds-v3.0.2 from the frozen RDS RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1, in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §4.5, and can be regenerated with the notebook reports/rds_counts.ipynb in the same repository.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all alerts generated between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2026 (36 monthly generation cohorts, daily alert generation) with investigation outcomes observed up to the label cut-off of 28 February 2027. Before exclusions the population contains 466,900 alerts on 311,480 unique customers, of which 44,250 (9.48%) were productive; after the exclusions in section 4.2 the RDS contains 457,260 alerts on 306,910 unique customers with 43,512 productive alerts (9.52%), of which 18,006 resulted in an unusual transaction report (MOT) to FIU-Nederland. The development window (alerts generated January 2024 – December 2025) contains 298,410 alerts with 27,640 productive alerts (9.26%) and the out-of-time window (January – December 2026) contains 158,850 alerts with 15,872 productive alerts (9.99%). Alert volumes grew from 148,900 in 2024 to 155,600 in 2025 and 162,400 in 2026, driven by customer growth and by the introduction of scenario S14 (money-mule indicators) in April 2024.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts on 1 January 2024 because the case management system FCM-CM was migrated to a new disposition code set on that date; alerts before 2024 carry disposition codes that cannot be mapped reliably to the productive-alert definition and were therefore not used. Three years of alerts cover two complete annual tuning cycles of the scenario thresholds (2024 and 2025) and the full production period of the logistic prioritisation model of version 2.0, which is used as the benchmark in the MDD. The most recent twelve months of outcomes (alerts generated in 2026) form the out-of-time sample and were set aside on 12 March 2027, before any feature selection or hyperparameter tuning; the development window was split into training (80%) and test (20%) samples grouped by customer, so that no customer appears in more than one sample. The window does not include a period of materially different money-laundering typologies; the typology shift identified by FIU-Nederland in 2025 (growth of instant-payment money-mule networks) is represented in both the development and the out-of-time window.

sections.heading: Target variable
sections.text: MDL-15 does not use a default-based target. In accordance with Annex A of MRM-STD-021, chapter 3 documents the target variable in section 3.1, and sections 3.3 and 3.4 are retained with the statement Not applicable. The label is derived from the investigation outcome recorded by Transaction Monitoring Operations and the FIU Reporting team in the case management system FCM-CM; it is not derived from any model output.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: An alert is labelled productive (target = 1) where the Level-1 analyst escalated it to a Level-2 case investigation or where it contributed to an unusual transaction report to FIU-Nederland, consistent with the definition of productive alert in FEC-STD-600 §3; all other dispositioned alerts are labelled non-productive (target = 0). The outcome horizon is the period between alert generation and final disposition; 99.1% of alerts generated in 2024–2026 reached final disposition within 60 days, and all alerts generated up to 31 December 2026 had an observable outcome at the label cut-off of 28 February 2027 except the 1,140 open alerts excluded in section 4.2. Every Level-1 and Level-2 decision in FCM-CM records the disposition code, the analyst's narrative with the considerations and conclusion, the evidence reviewed and the four-eyes approval for closures of alerts on High-risk customers, so that each label can be traced to a documented decision. To prevent target leakage, features are computed only from data available at the alert generation timestamp; post-alert information such as case notes, requests for information to the customer, account restrictions or exit decisions is excluded from the feature set.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable: MDL-15 does not use the default definition of CR-STD-110, so there are no deviations to document; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. The target variable of the prioritisation layer is the productive-alert label defined in section 3.1, which is governed by FEC-STD-600 rather than by the credit risk standards. Any future change in the definition of a productive alert, for example as a consequence of the FIU-Nederland reporting changes expected under the AMLR, will be treated as a target definition change under MRM-STD-050.

evidence.quote: Not applicable: MDL-15 does not use the default definition of CR-STD-110, so there are no deviations to document; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: Not applicable: the model does not estimate default probabilities and does not use days-past-due counting, materiality thresholds, probation periods or historical approximations of a default flag. The equivalent information for the productive-alert label, including the treatment of the disposition code migration in January 2024, is documented in sections 3.1 and 6.2 (data deficiency DD-TM-01). The label is observed at alert level and not at customer level, so a customer with several alerts in the observation period contributes several observations; this is taken into account by grouping the train–test split by customer.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable: unlikeliness-to-pay triggers relate to the credit risk default definition and have no counterpart in the transaction monitoring target. The escalation triggers that determine a productive label (escalation to Level 2, contribution to an MOT) are defined in the Transaction Monitoring Operations procedure TMO-PRC-004 version 5.2 and summarised in section 3.1. Changes to that procedure during the observation period (version 5.0 in January 2024 and version 5.2 in May 2025) did not change the escalation criteria.

sections.heading: Label quality and feedback-loop bias
sections.text: Because the labels reflect past analyst decisions on alerts that were prioritised by the version 2.0 model, the RDS is exposed to feedback-loop bias: alerts ranked low by the previous model were handled later and by less experienced analysts, which may have depressed their productive rate. The effect was assessed by comparing the productive rate of low-ranked alerts handled by senior analysts (8.7%) with that of low-ranked alerts handled by junior analysts (7.9%) in 2025; the difference of 0.8 percentage points is significant at 5% and is recorded as limitation L-TM-01 in the MDD. Since January 2026 a random sample of 2% of all alerts in the two lowest priority bands has been reviewed each month by senior analysts irrespective of their score; the 1,420 sampled alerts of 2026 are included in the RDS with a sample flag and are used to estimate the unbiased productive rate in the low-priority bands. Label consistency was tested through a blind re-review of 600 closed alerts by the Transaction Monitoring QA team in November 2026, which confirmed the original disposition in 96.3% of cases.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: Chapter 4 describes the sources, lineage, exclusions and treatment of missing values and outliers. The RDS combines alert data from the TMX platform with transaction, customer and case data that were available at the alert timestamp. The full list of 58 RDS variables (46 model features, the target, the alert key and ten control and sampling attributes) with their definitions and lineage is given in Annex A.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from seven source systems mapped to four data domains in the Group Data Catalogue: Payments (Payments Hub for SEPA credit transfers, SEPA Instant and direct debits; SWIFT gateway for international payments; Card Transaction Store), Cash (Cash Management System, including deposits at Geldmaat machines), Customer (KYC platform KYC-One and Customer Master Data) and FEC Case (TMX platform and case management system FCM-CM). Each domain has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: the Head of Payments Operations (Payments), the Head of Cash Services (Cash), the Head of Client Data Management (Customer) and the Head of Transaction Monitoring Operations (FEC Case). Data are extracted daily at 02:00 CET from the source systems into the FEC Data Hub (FDH), transformed by the dbt project fdh-tm (jobs fdh_tm_txn_daily, fdh_tm_cust_daily and fdh_tm_alert_daily) into the curated schema FDH.TM_CURATED, and aggregated into alert-level features by the feature pipeline tm-features in repository fec-analytics/tm-rds. Annex A documents for every model variable, including the 17 discarded variables used to construct retained variables, the source system and field, each intermediate data store, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the dbt model or Python function, and the extraction frequency and timing. All products and payment channels of a business relationship feed the same customer-level features, so that monitoring covers current accounts, savings accounts, cards, cash and international payments of the customer together.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions were applied, each quantified by the build code: (a) 6,120 technical duplicate alerts (1.31% of alerts, 412 productive) generated twice by platform re-runs after incidents INC-2024-3381 and INC-2025-0912, where the original alert is retained; (b) 2,380 alerts (0.51%, 326 productive) on customers of the discontinued Belgian branch, whose run-off was completed in September 2025 and which are no longer in the model's range of application; (c) 1,140 alerts (0.24%) with an open disposition at the label cut-off. The impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that exclusions (a) and (c) do not affect representativeness and that exclusion (b), which removes 6.2% of the alerts of segment RP-H, does not bias the current-portfolio representativeness because the branch population no longer exists. Because exclusion (b) exceeds 5% of the records of segment RP-H, it was approved by the model owner on 10 March 2027 and reported to Model Validation – Financial Crime on 11 March 2027. No exclusions were applied at scenario level: alerts from all 17 scenarios active during the observation period and from the Wwft objective-indicator rules are included, with the objective-indicator alerts flagged because they are not scored by the prioritisation model.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are documented per variable in Annex C and classified as missing for a structural reason (for example no previous alerts for a new customer, encoded as zero with an indicator), missing at random (0.4% of card merchant country codes) or missing because of a data deficiency (expected monthly turnover missing for 6.8% of SB-1 customers, DD-TM-02). Missing expected turnover is imputed with the median of the customer's peer group (segment and SBI industry section) calculated on the development window, a missing-indicator feature is added, and 2.9% of alerts carry an imputed value; re-estimation without imputation reduced the out-of-time Gini by 0.3 percentage points, which is recorded in section 7.4 of the MDD. Outliers are identified with a documented rule applied identically in development and production: continuous amount and ratio features are capped at the 99.9th percentile of the development window per segment, and the caps are stored in the versioned parameter file feature_caps_v3.yaml. Capping affects 0.1% of values per feature by construction, and its impact on model output is below 0.1 percentage point of Gini on the test sample. The target variable is never imputed: the 1,140 alerts without a final disposition are excluded (section 4.2) and 37 alerts with contradictory disposition codes were corrected at source in FCM-CM by Transaction Monitoring Operations under ticket FEC-DQ-2027-014 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Manual interventions and external data
sections.text: The only manual intervention in the data flow is the upload of the internal Country Risk Matrix, which Financial Crime Compliance maintains as a spreadsheet and uploads quarterly to FDH; the upload is controlled by four-eyes approval, a checksum comparison with the approved version and an automated comparison with the EU list of high-risk third countries. External data enter the lineage at the point of receipt within the Bank: the EU list of high-risk third countries under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675 (as amended, version applied recorded per load date), SBI industry codes from the Chamber of Commerce (KvK) trade register (monthly delivery, delivery date recorded) and crypto-asset service provider identifiers from the DNB and ESMA registers (weekly delivery). Changes to the Country Risk Matrix or to the source definition of any data element are approved by the Data Owner and notified to the model owner at least one month before they take effect, in accordance with the data sharing agreement DSA-FEC-2025-03.

Lineage is recorded in the Group Data Catalogue at variable level and exported with every RDS version.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Chapter 5 compares the RDS with the alert population the model will score in production, on feature distributions and on productive-alert rates, and assesses the effect of the exclusions and of the threshold changes introduced in version 3.0. Detailed tables per segment, scenario group and feature are given in Annex B. The reference population for the comparison is the alert population of January and February 2027, which was scored in the pre-production environment but not used for development.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was tested against the alerts generated in January and February 2027 (27,410 alerts): the PSI of the score is 0.03, the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.07 and no feature exceeds 0.10. The productive rate of the reference period (10.2%, 95% interval 9.8%–10.6% on matured alerts) is not significantly different from that of the out-of-time sample (9.99%), and the mix of scenario groups and segments differs by less than two percentage points per category. Segment CO-1 is small (3,900 alerts in the RDS) and its productive rate varies considerably between years (6.1% to 9.4%); this is recorded as limitation L-TM-03 in the MDD.

evidence.quote: Representativeness was tested against the alerts generated in January and February 2027 (27,410 alerts): the PSI of the score is 0.03, the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.07 and no feature exceeds 0.10.

The productive rate of the reference period (10.2%, 95% interval 9.8%–10.6% on matured alerts) is not significantly different from that of the out-of-time sample (9.99%), and the mix of scenario groups and segments differs by less than two percentage points per category.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: Version 3.0 lowers the thresholds of scenarios S02, S06, S07 and S14 and introduces scenario S18 (unusual loan repayments). Alerts generated in the newly covered region below the version 2.0 thresholds, estimated at 4.1% of the future alert volume, are not represented in the RDS because they were not alerted in the observation period. For these alerts the representativeness was approximated with the 660 below-the-line test events of scenarios S02, S06, S07 and S14 in the 2026 testing cycle (EVD-15-ATL), which were reviewed by analysts and labelled; the productive rate of these events (2.6%) is within the range of the three lowest scored deciles of the RDS. Because this approximation is based on a small sample, alerts from lowered thresholds and from S18 are excluded from the auto-closure band for twelve months after go-live (limitation L-TM-02).

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Excluding technical duplicates (a) changes no feature distribution by more than PSI 0.001 and reduces the productive rate by 0.04 percentage points; retaining the original alert of each duplicate pair preserves the information content. Excluding the Belgian branch alerts (b) lowers the productive rate of segment RP-H from 11.9% to 11.3%; since the branch population was wound down in 2025 the excluded alerts are not representative of the current portfolio, and including them would have overstated the RP-H productive rate. Excluding open alerts (c) could bias the label if long-running investigations are more often productive; 34% of the open alerts had been escalated to Level 2 at the cut-off. A sensitivity analysis treating all escalated open alerts as productive changes the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage point.

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Chapter 6 reports the data quality assessment of the RDS under MRM-STD-022 and the data deficiencies identified. The recurring production data quality controls on the TM data feeds are reported separately in the data quality report EVD-15-DQ. All data quality rules referenced in this chapter are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool under rule set DQ-FEC-TM-v3, and their results for the RDS are stored with the frozen RDS so that the assessment can be repeated by Model Validation.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development on 8 March 2027 on the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness for all 58 critical data elements, which comprise every model feature, the productive label and its constituents (disposition code, escalation flag and MOT reference). Completeness is measured at record level (all alerts of the TMX alert log present in the RDS: 466,900 of 466,900) and at attribute level (share of non-missing values per variable, at least 99.2% for all features except expected monthly turnover of SB-1 customers at 93.2%). Accuracy was measured by reconciling transaction counts and amounts per month to the Payments Hub and Cash Management System (maximum difference 0.06% of amount) and by a sample-based check of 400 alerts against source documentation in FCM-CM and the original payment messages, in which 399 alerts matched. Consistency was tested between the RDS and the production feature store on the same reference dates (identical for 99.97% of feature values), over time across the disposition code migration of January 2024, and through 41 logical rules such as alert date not preceding account opening date. Timeliness is measured as the lag between transaction booking and availability in FDH (T+1 for all feeds except Geldmaat cash deposits at T+2) and as the currency of CDD data, where 97.8% of customers had a CDD review within the interval required for their risk class. The assessment reports the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its amber and red thresholds together with the number and share of excluded records per exclusion reason, concludes that the RDS is fit for the development of the prioritisation model, and was signed off by the lead developer and the model owner on 12 March 2027 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: For every critical data element at least one rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension; timeliness is recorded as not applicable to static attributes such as account opening date, with the reason stated in the rule set. The rules and their thresholds are documented in RDS Annex C and implemented as recurring checks in the Group DQ monitoring tool, rule set DQ-FEC-TM-v3 (212 rules). Each rule has an amber and a red threshold; the MRM-STD-022 defaults are applied (completeness amber below 98% and red below 95% non-missing, accuracy amber above 0.5% and red above 1% difference, consistency amber below 99% and red below 98% passing), and stricter thresholds apply to transaction amount reconciliation, where the FEC-STD-600 §12.1 tolerance of 0.1% is used as the amber threshold. The label constituents (disposition code, escalation flag and MOT reference) are subject to thresholds at least as strict as the defaults, with completeness red below 99.5%.

sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of customers and counterparties, including data relating to suspected criminal offences, and is therefore subject to PRIV-POL-001 and the GDPR. Sections 7.1 to 7.5 document the lawful basis, the minimisation, the DPIA, the security and pseudonymisation measures and the retention periods; section 7.6 documents the exclusion of protected attributes and the proxy screening. The processing complies with AI-POL-001 §4.7: data protection by design and data minimisation are applied to the prioritisation layer as described below.

sections.heading: Lawful basis and purpose
sections.text: The processing of customer, transaction and alert data for transaction monitoring, including the development, validation and application of MDL-15, is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, as it is necessary for compliance with the Bank's legal obligations under Articles 2a, 3 and 16 of the Wwft, and is recorded in the Record of Processing under RoP-0412 (Transaction monitoring) and RoP-0413 (FEC model development and validation) before processing started. The purposes are specified and explicit: detection of unusual transactions for reporting to FIU-Nederland and the development, validation and monitoring of the models that support it; the data are not used for credit, marketing or pricing purposes. Reuse of the historical alert and case data, originally collected for the investigation of individual alerts, for model development was assessed in compatibility assessment CA-2024-007 against the Art. 6(4)(a)–(e) factors (link between purposes, context, nature of the data, consequences and safeguards), concluding that the purposes are compatible. The Bank does not rely on legitimate interests under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR for this processing, so no legitimate interest assessment is required. Data relating to suspected criminal offences (alert dispositions and MOT references) are processed only as authorised by the Wwft as Member State law (Art. 10 GDPR), and customers are informed of the monitoring through the Bank's privacy statement. RoP-0412 and RoP-0413 record the purposes, the data categories, the recipients (FIU-Nederland for MOTs, Model Validation and Internal Audit internally), the absence of transfers outside the EEA and the retention periods, and the Model Inventory and AI Inventory records reference both entries.

sections.heading: Personal data attributes and minimisation
sections.text: The RDS contains 31 personal data attributes, each justified by its relevance to the detection purpose in Annex A (for example the expected monthly turnover recorded at CDD, the CRR class and the counterparty country of payments); customer names, addresses, dates of birth, nationality and free-text payment descriptions are not included. For each attribute Annex A lists its purpose in the model, the lawful basis (Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR with the Wwft), the pseudonymisation applied (customer, account and counterparty identifiers replaced by keyed tokens) and the retention period of section 7.5. Only data obtained under customer due diligence and transaction data of the Bank are used; no external personal data such as social media or data broker information are processed by the model. No special categories of personal data within the meaning of Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed in the RDS or by the model, and no Art. 9(2) exception is relied upon; payment descriptions that could reveal such data (for example donations to religious organisations or payments to healthcare providers) are not used as features.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.text: Customer due diligence data, transaction records and alert investigation records are retained for five years after the end of the business relationship or the occasional transaction, and MOT data for five years after the report, in accordance with Articles 33 and 34 of the Wwft and, from 10 July 2027, Article 77 AMLR. The RDS and development snapshots are retained in identifiable (pseudonymised) form for the period of use of the model and five years after its decommissioning, in accordance with PRIV-POL-001 §10.2. At the end of that period the token keys and all records that permit re-identification are destroyed, so that the archived RDS is irreversibly anonymised; deletion is evidenced by a deletion certificate of the data custodian recorded in the Model Inventory.

sections.heading: Protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Protected attributes (sex, age, nationality and country of birth) are not used as model features; they are held separately in the secure validation area for fairness testing only. All 46 features were screened for proxy effects against sex, age group and nationality group (Dutch, other EEA, non-EEA): 45 features predict none of these attributes with an AUC above 0.65 or a Cramér's V above 0.30. The feature hrc_flow_share_90d (share of payment value to or from higher-risk countries) predicts the non-EEA nationality group with an AUC of 0.68 and is retained because geographic risk is a legal risk factor under Wwft art. 8 and Annex III of Directive (EU) 2015/849; the retention was approved by the AI Governance Office on 24 February 2027 (decision AIGO-2027-009) and is recorded as expert judgement EJ-TM-07. The model does not evaluate or classify customers on the basis of social behaviour or personal characteristics outside the AML context: the score is used only to order alerts for investigation and is not shared with credit, pricing or marketing processes.

sections.heading: Annex B – Representativeness analyses
sections.text: Annex B contains the PSI of all 46 features and of the score between the development window, the out-of-time window and the January–February 2027 reference period, per segment and scenario group, as well as the comparison of missing-value shares. The highest feature PSI between the development and out-of-time windows is 0.09 for instant_share_debit_30d, reflecting the growth of SEPA Instant payments from 18% to 31% of retail debit transactions between 2024 and 2026. Productive rates per segment and scenario group are compared with two-sample tests of proportions at 5% significance; the only significant difference between the development and out-of-time windows is the higher productive rate of the typology group in 2026 (11.9% versus 10.4%), explained by the growth of money-mule alerts.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1 used to develop, test and validate version 3.0 of model MDL-15 AML Transaction Monitoring, specifically its machine-learning alert prioritisation layer, and it follows the RDS documentation template of Annex A to MRM-STD-021. MDL-15 generates alerts on potentially unusual transactions of retail and business payment customers of the Bank through 18 rules-based detection scenarios and ranks those alerts with a gradient-boosted prioritisation model; the model is registered in the Model Inventory as a Tier 1 FEC model and is used to meet the Bank's transaction monitoring obligations under the Wwft and, from its date of application on 10 July 2027, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR). The scope of application comprises all natural persons, sole proprietors, small and medium-sized enterprises and corporate customers holding payment accounts with the Bank in the Netherlands; institutional and correspondent banking relationships are monitored by a separate model and are outside the scope of this RDS. The model is developed in-house by FEC Analytics; the scenario logic runs on a vendor rules engine (TMX platform, release 10.4) configured by the Bank, and the model is governed under MRM-POL-001 irrespective of the vendor component. The companion documents are the model development document EVD-15-MDD (TM scenario and tuning documentation), the data quality report EVD-15-DQ and the implementation and testing report EVD-15-IMPL.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: Chapter 2 describes the observation period of the alert-level RDS. The unit of observation is an alert generated by one of the TM scenarios in production and dispositioned by an analyst; the target is the investigation outcome of that alert as defined in chapter 3. All counts in chapters 2 to 6 are produced by the RDS build code at tag rds-v3.0.2 from the frozen RDS RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1, in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §4.5, and can be regenerated with the notebook reports/rds_counts.ipynb in the same repository.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all alerts generated between 1 January 2024 and 31 December 2026 (36 monthly generation cohorts, daily alert generation) with investigation outcomes observed up to the label cut-off of 28 February 2027. Before exclusions the population contains 466,900 alerts on 311,480 unique customers, of which 44,250 (9.48%) were productive; after the exclusions in section 4.2 the RDS contains 457,260 alerts on 306,910 unique customers with 43,512 productive alerts (9.52%), of which 18,006 resulted in an unusual transaction report (MOT) to FIU-Nederland. The development window (alerts generated January 2024 – December 2025) contains 298,410 alerts with 27,640 productive alerts (9.26%) and the out-of-time window (January – December 2026) contains 158,850 alerts with 15,872 productive alerts (9.99%). Alert volumes grew from 148,900 in 2024 to 155,600 in 2025 and 162,400 in 2026, driven by customer growth and by the introduction of scenario S14 (money-mule indicators) in April 2024.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts on 1 January 2024 because the case management system FCM-CM was migrated to a new disposition code set on that date; alerts before 2024 carry disposition codes that cannot be mapped reliably to the productive-alert definition and were therefore not used. Three years of alerts cover two complete annual tuning cycles of the scenario thresholds (2024 and 2025) and the full production period of the logistic prioritisation model of version 2.0, which is used as the benchmark in the MDD. The most recent twelve months of outcomes (alerts generated in 2026) form the out-of-time sample and were set aside on 12 March 2027, before any feature selection or hyperparameter tuning; the development window was split into training (80%) and test (20%) samples grouped by customer, so that no customer appears in more than one sample. The window does not include a period of materially different money-laundering typologies; the typology shift identified by FIU-Nederland in 2025 (growth of instant-payment money-mule networks) is represented in both the development and the out-of-time window.

sections.heading: Target variable
sections.text: MDL-15 does not use a default-based target. In accordance with Annex A of MRM-STD-021, chapter 3 documents the target variable in section 3.1, and sections 3.3 and 3.4 are retained with the statement Not applicable. The label is derived from the investigation outcome recorded by Transaction Monitoring Operations and the FIU Reporting team in the case management system FCM-CM; it is not derived from any model output.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: An alert is labelled productive (target = 1) where the Level-1 analyst escalated it to a Level-2 case investigation or where it contributed to an unusual transaction report to FIU-Nederland, consistent with the definition of productive alert in FEC-STD-600 §3; all other dispositioned alerts are labelled non-productive (target = 0). The outcome horizon is the period between alert generation and final disposition; 99.1% of alerts generated in 2024–2026 reached final disposition within 60 days, and all alerts generated up to 31 December 2026 had an observable outcome at the label cut-off of 28 February 2027 except the 1,140 open alerts excluded in section 4.2. Every Level-1 and Level-2 decision in FCM-CM records the disposition code, the analyst's narrative with the considerations and conclusion, the evidence reviewed and the four-eyes approval for closures of alerts on High-risk customers, so that each label can be traced to a documented decision. To prevent target leakage, features are computed only from data available at the alert generation timestamp; post-alert information such as case notes, requests for information to the customer, account restrictions or exit decisions is excluded from the feature set.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable: MDL-15 does not use the default definition of CR-STD-110, so there are no deviations to document; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. The target variable of the prioritisation layer is the productive-alert label defined in section 3.1, which is governed by FEC-STD-600 rather than by the credit risk standards. Any future change in the definition of a productive alert, for example as a consequence of the FIU-Nederland reporting changes expected under the AMLR, will be treated as a target definition change under MRM-STD-050.

evidence.quote: Not applicable: MDL-15 does not use the default definition of CR-STD-110, so there are no deviations to document; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: Not applicable: the model does not estimate default probabilities and does not use days-past-due counting, materiality thresholds, probation periods or historical approximations of a default flag. The equivalent information for the productive-alert label, including the treatment of the disposition code migration in January 2024, is documented in sections 3.1 and 6.2 (data deficiency DD-TM-01). The label is observed at alert level and not at customer level, so a customer with several alerts in the observation period contributes several observations; this is taken into account by grouping the train–test split by customer.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable: unlikeliness-to-pay triggers relate to the credit risk default definition and have no counterpart in the transaction monitoring target. The escalation triggers that determine a productive label (escalation to Level 2, contribution to an MOT) are defined in the Transaction Monitoring Operations procedure TMO-PRC-004 version 5.2 and summarised in section 3.1. Changes to that procedure during the observation period (version 5.0 in January 2024 and version 5.2 in May 2025) did not change the escalation criteria.

sections.heading: Label quality and feedback-loop bias
sections.text: Because the labels reflect past analyst decisions on alerts that were prioritised by the version 2.0 model, the RDS is exposed to feedback-loop bias: alerts ranked low by the previous model were handled later and by less experienced analysts, which may have depressed their productive rate. The effect was assessed by comparing the productive rate of low-ranked alerts handled by senior analysts (8.7%) with that of low-ranked alerts handled by junior analysts (7.9%) in 2025; the difference of 0.8 percentage points is significant at 5% and is recorded as limitation L-TM-01 in the MDD. Since January 2026 a random sample of 2% of all alerts in the two lowest priority bands has been reviewed each month by senior analysts irrespective of their score; the 1,420 sampled alerts of 2026 are included in the RDS with a sample flag and are used to estimate the unbiased productive rate in the low-priority bands. Label consistency was tested through a blind re-review of 600 closed alerts by the Transaction Monitoring QA team in November 2026, which confirmed the original disposition in 96.3% of cases.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: Chapter 4 describes the sources, lineage, exclusions and treatment of missing values and outliers. The RDS combines alert data from the TMX platform with transaction, customer and case data that were available at the alert timestamp. The full list of 58 RDS variables (46 model features, the target, the alert key and ten control and sampling attributes) with their definitions and lineage is given in Annex A.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from seven source systems mapped to four data domains in the Group Data Catalogue: Payments (Payments Hub for SEPA credit transfers, SEPA Instant and direct debits; SWIFT gateway for international payments; Card Transaction Store), Cash (Cash Management System, including deposits at Geldmaat machines), Customer (KYC platform KYC-One and Customer Master Data) and FEC Case (TMX platform and case management system FCM-CM). Each domain has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: the Head of Payments Operations (Payments), the Head of Cash Services (Cash), the Head of Client Data Management (Customer) and the Head of Transaction Monitoring Operations (FEC Case). Data are extracted daily at 02:00 CET from the source systems into the FEC Data Hub (FDH), transformed by the dbt project fdh-tm (jobs fdh_tm_txn_daily, fdh_tm_cust_daily and fdh_tm_alert_daily) into the curated schema FDH.TM_CURATED, and aggregated into alert-level features by the feature pipeline tm-features in repository fec-analytics/tm-rds. Annex A documents for every model variable, including the 17 discarded variables used to construct retained variables, the source system and field, each intermediate data store, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the dbt model or Python function, and the extraction frequency and timing. All products and payment channels of a business relationship feed the same customer-level features, so that monitoring covers current accounts, savings accounts, cards, cash and international payments of the customer together.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Three exclusions were applied, each quantified by the build code: (a) 6,120 technical duplicate alerts (1.31% of alerts, 412 productive) generated twice by platform re-runs after incidents INC-2024-3381 and INC-2025-0912, where the original alert is retained; (b) 2,380 alerts (0.51%, 326 productive) on customers of the discontinued Belgian branch, whose run-off was completed in September 2025 and which are no longer in the model's range of application; (c) 1,140 alerts (0.24%) with an open disposition at the label cut-off. The impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that exclusions (a) and (c) do not affect representativeness and that exclusion (b), which removes 6.2% of the alerts of segment RP-H, does not bias the current-portfolio representativeness because the branch population no longer exists. Because exclusion (b) exceeds 5% of the records of segment RP-H, it was approved by the model owner on 10 March 2027 and reported to Model Validation – Financial Crime on 11 March 2027. No exclusions were applied at scenario level: alerts from all 17 scenarios active during the observation period and from the Wwft objective-indicator rules are included, with the objective-indicator alerts flagged because they are not scored by the prioritisation model.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are documented per variable in Annex C and classified as missing for a structural reason (for example no previous alerts for a new customer, encoded as zero with an indicator), missing at random (0.4% of card merchant country codes) or missing because of a data deficiency (expected monthly turnover missing for 6.8% of SB-1 customers, DD-TM-02). Missing expected turnover is imputed with the median of the customer's peer group (segment and SBI industry section) calculated on the development window, a missing-indicator feature is added, and 2.9% of alerts carry an imputed value; re-estimation without imputation reduced the out-of-time Gini by 0.3 percentage points, which is recorded in section 7.4 of the MDD. Outliers are identified with a documented rule applied identically in development and production: continuous amount and ratio features are capped at the 99.9th percentile of the development window per segment, and the caps are stored in the versioned parameter file feature_caps_v3.yaml. Capping affects 0.1% of values per feature by construction, and its impact on model output is below 0.1 percentage point of Gini on the test sample. The target variable is never imputed: the 1,140 alerts without a final disposition are excluded (section 4.2) and 37 alerts with contradictory disposition codes were corrected at source in FCM-CM by Transaction Monitoring Operations under ticket FEC-DQ-2027-014 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Manual interventions and external data
sections.text: The only manual intervention in the data flow is the upload of the internal Country Risk Matrix, which Financial Crime Compliance maintains as a spreadsheet and uploads quarterly to FDH; the upload is controlled by four-eyes approval, a checksum comparison with the approved version and an automated comparison with the EU list of high-risk third countries. External data enter the lineage at the point of receipt within the Bank: the EU list of high-risk third countries under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675 (as amended, version applied recorded per load date), SBI industry codes from the Chamber of Commerce (KvK) trade register (monthly delivery, delivery date recorded) and crypto-asset service provider identifiers from the DNB and ESMA registers (weekly delivery). Changes to the Country Risk Matrix or to the source definition of any data element are approved by the Data Owner and notified to the model owner at least one month before they take effect, in accordance with the data sharing agreement DSA-FEC-2025-03.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Chapter 5 compares the RDS with the alert population the model will score in production, on feature distributions and on productive-alert rates, and assesses the effect of the exclusions and of the threshold changes introduced in version 3.0. Detailed tables per segment, scenario group and feature are given in Annex B. The reference population for the comparison is the alert population of January and February 2027, which was scored in the pre-production environment but not used for development.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness was tested against the alerts generated in January and February 2027 (27,410 alerts): the PSI of the score is 0.03, the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.07 and no feature exceeds 0.10. The productive rate of the reference period (10.2%, 95% interval 9.8%–10.6% on matured alerts) is not significantly different from that of the out-of-time sample (9.99%), and the mix of scenario groups and segments differs by less than two percentage points per category. Segment CO-1 is small (3,900 alerts in the RDS) and its productive rate varies considerably between years (6.1% to 9.4%); this is recorded as limitation L-TM-03 in the MDD.

evidence.quote: Representativeness was tested against the alerts generated in January and February 2027 (27,410 alerts): the PSI of the score is 0.03, the PSI of the ten most important features ranges from 0.01 to 0.07 and no feature exceeds 0.10.

The productive rate of the reference period (10.2%, 95% interval 9.8%–10.6% on matured alerts) is not significantly different from that of the out-of-time sample (9.99%), and the mix of scenario groups and segments differs by less than two percentage points per category.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: Version 3.0 lowers the thresholds of scenarios S02, S06, S07 and S14 and introduces scenario S18 (unusual loan repayments). Alerts generated in the newly covered region below the version 2.0 thresholds, estimated at 4.1% of the future alert volume, are not represented in the RDS because they were not alerted in the observation period. For these alerts the representativeness was approximated with the 660 below-the-line test events of scenarios S02, S06, S07 and S14 in the 2026 testing cycle (EVD-15-ATL), which were reviewed by analysts and labelled; the productive rate of these events (2.6%) is within the range of the three lowest scored deciles of the RDS. Because this approximation is based on a small sample, alerts from lowered thresholds and from S18 are excluded from the auto-closure band for twelve months after go-live (limitation L-TM-02).

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Excluding technical duplicates (a) changes no feature distribution by more than PSI 0.001 and reduces the productive rate by 0.04 percentage points; retaining the original alert of each duplicate pair preserves the information content. Excluding the Belgian branch alerts (b) lowers the productive rate of segment RP-H from 11.9% to 11.3%; since the branch population was wound down in 2025 the excluded alerts are not representative of the current portfolio, and including them would have overstated the RP-H productive rate. Excluding open alerts (c) could bias the label if long-running investigations are more often productive; 34% of the open alerts had been escalated to Level 2 at the cut-off. A sensitivity analysis treating all escalated open alerts as productive changes the out-of-time Gini by less than 0.1 percentage point.

sections.heading: Bias analysis of the development data
sections.text: The analysis of bias in the data covers historical decision bias (the feedback-loop effect of section 3.5), label bias from differences in analyst experience, under-representation of segment CO-1 and of the 18–24 age band in business segments, and measurement bias from the imputed expected turnover of legacy SB-1 customers. Mitigation measures are the 2% random low-priority review, the exclusion of CO-1 alerts from auto-closure, the missing-indicator feature for imputed expected turnover and the monitoring of fairness metrics per age group and sex; after mitigation, including an interaction constraint on account age, the adverse-impact ratio across age groups improved from 0.78 (candidate model) to 0.84. Protected attributes are available only in the secure validation area for fairness testing and are not part of the feature set (chapter 7).

sections.heading: Data quality
sections.text: Chapter 6 reports the data quality assessment of the RDS under MRM-STD-022 and the data deficiencies identified. The recurring production data quality controls on the TM data feeds are reported separately in the data quality report EVD-15-DQ. All data quality rules referenced in this chapter are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool under rule set DQ-FEC-TM-v3, and their results for the RDS are stored with the frozen RDS so that the assessment can be repeated by Model Validation.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development on 8 March 2027 on the dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness for all 58 critical data elements, which comprise every model feature, the productive label and its constituents (disposition code, escalation flag and MOT reference). Completeness is measured at record level (all alerts of the TMX alert log present in the RDS: 466,900 of 466,900) and at attribute level (share of non-missing values per variable, at least 99.2% for all features except expected monthly turnover of SB-1 customers at 93.2%). Accuracy was measured by reconciling transaction counts and amounts per month to the Payments Hub and Cash Management System (maximum difference 0.06% of amount) and by a sample-based check of 400 alerts against source documentation in FCM-CM and the original payment messages, in which 399 alerts matched. Consistency was tested between the RDS and the production feature store on the same reference dates (identical for 99.97% of feature values), over time across the disposition code migration of January 2024, and through 41 logical rules such as alert date not preceding account opening date. Timeliness is measured as the lag between transaction booking and availability in FDH (T+1 for all feeds except Geldmaat cash deposits at T+2) and as the currency of CDD data, where 97.8% of customers had a CDD review within the interval required for their risk class. The assessment reports the result of each rule per variable and dimension against its amber and red thresholds together with the number and share of excluded records per exclusion reason, concludes that the RDS is fit for the development of the prioritisation model, and was signed off by the lead developer and the model owner on 12 March 2027 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: Five deficiencies are recorded in the model's data deficiency log, each with affected variables and segments, dimension, cause, impact and treatment: DD-TM-01 disposition code migration January–June 2024 (consistency, 71,300 alerts, treated by a version-controlled mapping table, limitation L-TM-08); DD-TM-02 missing expected turnover for 6.8% of SB-1 customers (completeness, treated by imputation, limitation L-TM-05); DD-TM-03 manual upload of the Country Risk Matrix (accuracy risk, treated by upload controls, limitation L-TM-06); DD-TM-04 Geldmaat cash feed lag and a 0.14% count difference in March 2025 (timeliness and accuracy, corrected at source); DD-TM-05 missing counterparty country for 2.3% of SEPA Instant transactions (completeness, derived from the IBAN country code, limitation L-TM-07). Each deficiency has a remediation owner and a target date: DD-TM-02 is being remediated at source through the CDD remediation programme of Client Data Management (target 31 December 2027) rather than only in the model data, and DD-TM-04 was closed on 30 June 2025 after confirmed remediation by Cash Services. The deficiencies are recorded in the Bank data issue register under DIR-2024-0712, DIR-2025-0233, DIR-2025-0419, DIR-2025-0145 and DIR-2026-0088. None of the deficiencies is rated high or critical, so no escalation to the Group Data Governance Committee or to the Model Risk Committee was required; the March 2025 red reconciliation breach on the Geldmaat feed was escalated to Model Risk Management within ten business days as required for a critical data element of a Tier 1 model. The mapping of old to new disposition codes (DD-TM-01) is not supported by source evidence for 640 alerts with ambiguous codes and is therefore documented and approved as expert judgement EJ-TM-06 in the expert judgement log, cross-referenced to this deficiency.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: For every critical data element at least one rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension; timeliness is recorded as not applicable to static attributes such as account opening date, with the reason stated in the rule set. The rules and their thresholds are documented in RDS Annex C and implemented as recurring checks in the Group DQ monitoring tool, rule set DQ-FEC-TM-v3 (212 rules). Each rule has an amber and a red threshold; the MRM-STD-022 defaults are applied (completeness amber below 98% and red below 95% non-missing, accuracy amber above 0.5% and red above 1% difference, consistency amber below 99% and red below 98% passing), and stricter thresholds apply to transaction amount reconciliation, where the FEC-STD-600 §12.1 tolerance of 0.1% is used as the amber threshold. The label constituents (disposition code, escalation flag and MOT reference) are subject to thresholds at least as strict as the defaults, with completeness red below 99.5%.

sections.heading: Personal data and fair treatment
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of customers and counterparties, including data relating to suspected criminal offences, and is therefore subject to PRIV-POL-001 and the GDPR. Sections 7.1 to 7.5 document the lawful basis, the minimisation, the DPIA, the security and pseudonymisation measures and the retention periods; section 7.6 documents the exclusion of protected attributes and the proxy screening. The processing complies with AI-POL-001 §4.7: data protection by design and data minimisation are applied to the prioritisation layer as described below.

sections.heading: Lawful basis and purpose
sections.text: The processing of customer, transaction and alert data for transaction monitoring, including the development, validation and application of MDL-15, is based on Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR, as it is necessary for compliance with the Bank's legal obligations under Articles 2a, 3 and 16 of the Wwft, and is recorded in the Record of Processing under RoP-0412 (Transaction monitoring) and RoP-0413 (FEC model development and validation) before processing started. The purposes are specified and explicit: detection of unusual transactions for reporting to FIU-Nederland and the development, validation and monitoring of the models that support it; the data are not used for credit, marketing or pricing purposes. Reuse of the historical alert and case data, originally collected for the investigation of individual alerts, for model development was assessed in compatibility assessment CA-2024-007 against the Art. 6(4)(a)–(e) factors (link between purposes, context, nature of the data, consequences and safeguards), concluding that the purposes are compatible. The Bank does not rely on legitimate interests under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR for this processing, so no legitimate interest assessment is required. Data relating to suspected criminal offences (alert dispositions and MOT references) are processed only as authorised by the Wwft as Member State law (Art. 10 GDPR), and customers are informed of the monitoring through the Bank's privacy statement. RoP-0412 and RoP-0413 record the purposes, the data categories, the recipients (FIU-Nederland for MOTs, Model Validation and Internal Audit internally), the absence of transfers outside the EEA and the retention periods, and the Model Inventory and AI Inventory records reference both entries.

sections.heading: Personal data attributes and minimisation
sections.text: The RDS contains 31 personal data attributes, each justified by its relevance to the detection purpose in Annex A (for example the expected monthly turnover recorded at CDD, the CRR class and the counterparty country of payments); customer names, addresses, dates of birth, nationality and free-text payment descriptions are not included. For each attribute Annex A lists its purpose in the model, the lawful basis (Art. 6(1)(c) GDPR with the Wwft), the pseudonymisation applied (customer, account and counterparty identifiers replaced by keyed tokens) and the retention period of section 7.5. Only data obtained under customer due diligence and transaction data of the Bank are used; no external personal data such as social media or data broker information are processed by the model. No special categories of personal data within the meaning of Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed in the RDS or by the model, and no Art. 9(2) exception is relied upon; payment descriptions that could reveal such data (for example donations to religious organisations or payments to healthcare providers) are not used as features.

sections.heading: Data protection impact assessment
sections.text: The processing is covered by DPIA-2024-031 Transaction monitoring including ML alert prioritisation, which is mandatory under PRIV-POL-001 §7.2 because the model uses machine learning on personal data, classifies natural persons for decisions on further investigation and is Tier 1. The DPIA contains a systematic description of the processing and purposes, an assessment of necessity and proportionality, an assessment of the risks to data subjects (in particular unjustified investigation, discriminatory prioritisation and data breaches involving criminal-offence data) and the measures envisaged, including pseudonymisation, human review of every alert outside the auto-closure band and fairness monitoring. The DPIA was updated for version 3.0 on 18 February 2027 because of the new features and the auto-closure band, and the Data Protection Officer's advice of 1 March 2027 is documented in the DPIA; the DPIA is otherwise reviewed at least every three years. The residual risk was assessed as medium after mitigation, so prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens under Art. 36 GDPR was not required.

sections.heading: Pseudonymisation and security
sections.text: Development and validation use pseudonymised data: customer, account and counterparty identifiers are replaced by keyed HMAC-SHA256 tokens whose keys are held by the FEC data custodian in Data Management, separate from the TM Modelling team. The RDS is held only in the approved secure analytics environment FEC-SAE with role-based access limited to 11 named users of FEC Analytics and Model Validation – Financial Crime, encryption at rest and in transit, and logging of all queries.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.text: Customer due diligence data, transaction records and alert investigation records are retained for five years after the end of the business relationship or the occasional transaction, and MOT data for five years after the report, in accordance with Articles 33 and 34 of the Wwft and, from 10 July 2027, Article 77 AMLR. The RDS and development snapshots are retained in identifiable (pseudonymised) form for the period of use of the model and five years after its decommissioning, in accordance with PRIV-POL-001 §10.2. At the end of that period the token keys and all records that permit re-identification are destroyed, so that the archived RDS is irreversibly anonymised; deletion is evidenced by a deletion certificate of the data custodian recorded in the Model Inventory.

sections.heading: Protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Protected attributes (sex, age, nationality and country of birth) are not used as model features; they are held separately in the secure validation area for fairness testing only. All 46 features were screened for proxy effects against sex, age group and nationality group (Dutch, other EEA, non-EEA): 45 features predict none of these attributes with an AUC above 0.65 or a Cramér's V above 0.30. The feature hrc_flow_share_90d (share of payment value to or from higher-risk countries) predicts the non-EEA nationality group with an AUC of 0.68 and is retained because geographic risk is a legal risk factor under Wwft art. 8 and Annex III of Directive (EU) 2015/849; the retention was approved by the AI Governance Office on 24 February 2027 (decision AIGO-2027-009) and is recorded as expert judgement EJ-TM-07. The model does not evaluate or classify customers on the basis of social behaviour or personal characteristics outside the AML context: the score is used only to order alerts for investigation and is not shared with credit, pricing or marketing processes.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built by versioned code only: repository fec-analytics/tm-rds on the Bank's GitLab, build code tag rds-v3.0.2, with the source snapshots of FDH as at 28 February 2027 (transaction and customer tables) and 1 March 2027 (case and alert tables). The software environment is recorded in the lock file environment-rds.lock (Python 3.11.8, pandas 2.2.1, dbt-core 1.7.9, pyarrow 15.0.0), and the pipeline runs with fixed random seed 20270315 for the grouped train–test split. A full rebuild by the reviewer on 14 March 2027 from the source snapshots reproduced the frozen RDS exactly: 457,260 alerts and 43,512 productive alerts, with identical file hashes for all 58 variables. The frozen RDS is stored read-only in FEC-SAE under version identifier RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1, which is referenced in this document and in chapter 3 of the MDD; it is archived with the build code, lineage export and metadata so that the development data can be reproduced. The RDS was signed off by the model owner on 12 March 2027, before model estimation started on 15 March 2027, and the sign-off is recorded in the Model Inventory.

sections.heading: Annex B – Representativeness analyses
sections.text: Annex B contains the PSI of all 46 features and of the score between the development window, the out-of-time window and the January–February 2027 reference period, per segment and scenario group, as well as the comparison of missing-value shares. The highest feature PSI between the development and out-of-time windows is 0.09 for instant_share_debit_30d, reflecting the growth of SEPA Instant payments from 18% to 31% of retail debit transactions between 2024 and 2026. Productive rates per segment and scenario group are compared with two-sample tests of proportions at 5% significance; the only significant difference between the development and out-of-time windows is the higher productive rate of the typology group in 2026 (11.9% versus 10.4%), explained by the growth of money-mule alerts.

sections.heading: Annex C – Missing values, outliers and data quality rules
sections.text: Annex C lists per variable the share of missing values, their classification (structural, at random or data deficiency), the treatment applied, the share of imputed values, the outlier cap and the justification of each treatment, together with the data quality rules and thresholds per critical data element. Structural missing values (no prior alerts, no card, no international payments) account for most missing values and are encoded as zero with a missing indicator where the absence itself carries information.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This model development document (MDD) documents version 3.0 of MDL-15 AML Transaction Monitoring and follows the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in Annex B to MRM-STD-021. Cover block: title TM scenario and tuning documentation; model identifier MDL-15; model version 3.0; document version 0.9; status Draft; author S. Jansen (lead developer); reviewer R. Visser; approvers M. Bakker (model owner) and P. de Graaf (Head of FEC Analytics Modelling); approval date pending. The purpose of MDL-15 is to detect transactions and patterns of behaviour of retail and business payment customers that are unusual in relation to the customer's profile and risk, so that they can be assessed by analysts and, where the unusual nature is confirmed, reported to FIU-Nederland. The model monitors all transactions of the business relationship on an ongoing basis against the customer's due diligence information, expected transaction profile and risk class, and pays particular attention to unusual transaction patterns and to transaction types that by their nature carry a higher money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk, such as cash, rapid pass-through of funds and payments involving higher-risk jurisdictions. The intended use is the generation and prioritisation of alerts for Level-1 review; secondary uses are the provision of alert history as an input to the Customer Risk Rating (MDL-16) and to event-driven CDD reviews, and management information on scenario effectiveness for the SIRA. The model does not decide on reporting to FIU-Nederland, on exits or on account restrictions; those decisions are taken by analysts and by the FIU Reporting team.

sections.heading: Regulatory context
sections.text: The model is a key control for the Bank's obligations under Articles 2a, 3(2)(d), 8 and 16 of the Wwft and, from its date of application on 10 July 2027, Articles 26, 34 and 69 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), and it implements chapter 5 of the DNB Guidance on the Wwft and the Sanctions Act on transaction monitoring. Because the Bank's transaction volumes (on average 72 million transactions per month in 2026) do not permit manual monitoring, the Bank operates an automated monitoring system consisting of a substantiated set of detection scenarios with segment-specific threshold values, documented per scenario in section 2.4. Alerts are assessed against all relevant facts and information known to the Bank, and the Level-1 queue is ordered by the priority score so that the assessment of transactions with the highest risk is prioritised by urgency. The indicators of the Wwft Implementation Decree 2018 (Uitvoeringsbesluit Wwft 2018) for banks are implemented in full: the objective indicators are implemented as deterministic rules whose hits are reported without scoring (section 2.4.3), and the subjective indicator, grounds to suppose that a transaction may relate to money laundering or terrorist financing, underlies the scenario alerts and the analysts' assessment. The AMLR transition is tracked in project FEC-AMLR-2027; the scenario catalogue has been mapped to the AMLR provisions and no scenario change is required on the date of application, but the FIU-Nederland reporting format change is recorded as limitation L-TM-09.

sections.heading: AI Act assessment and AI Inventory
sections.text: The assessment against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act concludes that the scenario layer is not an AI system, because it applies fixed rules and thresholds defined by the Bank, whereas the prioritisation layer is an AI system, because it infers from alert, transaction and customer data how to generate predictions (priority scores) that influence the order of investigation. The use case is registered in the AI Inventory as AI-UC-2024-011, recording the purpose, the Use Case Owner and technical owner, the systems used, the Bank's role as provider and deployer, the affected persons (customers and counterparties), the data categories, the classifications and the Model Inventory identifier MDL-15. Under the AI Act the use case is classified as minimal risk: it is not a prohibited practice under Art. 5, AML transaction monitoring by a credit institution is not an Annex III use case, and customers do not interact directly with the system, so Art. 50 does not apply; the rationale was reviewed by the AI Governance Office on 24 February 2027. The internal AI Risk Class is Elevated, reflecting a Tier 1 model with material but indirect customer impact, human review of all alerts outside the auto-closure band and no automated customer decisions; the classification and AI Risk Class are reassessed at every material change, as for version 3.0, and at least annually. The system is not used for any practice prohibited by Art. 5 AI Act: it does not use manipulative techniques, does not exploit vulnerabilities and does not perform social scoring, because the score is used only within the AML process to order alerts and is never used to treat customers detrimentally in unrelated contexts.

sections.heading: Users, roles and lines of defence
sections.text: Transaction monitoring governance follows the three lines of defence: FEC Analytics (1LoD) develops and tunes the model, Transaction Monitoring Operations (1LoD) investigates alerts, Financial Crime Compliance (2LoD) approves coverage gaps, threshold rationales and BTL outcomes and decides on reports to FIU-Nederland, Model Validation – Financial Crime (2LoD) validates the model and Internal Audit (3LoD) audits the framework. The independent compliance function monitors the functioning of transaction monitoring and the timely reporting of unusual transactions to FIU-Nederland, and Internal Audit last audited transaction monitoring in audit IA-2026-FEC-07 (report of 30 September 2026, rating satisfactory with two medium findings, both closed). The model owner, M. Bakker, is the single accountable 1LoD senior manager recorded in the inventory and remains accountable for the tasks delegated to the TM Modelling team. The Bank has sufficient in-house understanding of the monitoring system: all scenario logic is specified, configured and tested by FEC Analytics, and the prioritisation model is developed in-house in Python; no vendor-supplied detection algorithm or vendor score is used. The criteria for the detection of unusual transactions, including scenario logic and thresholds, are approved by Financial Crime Compliance and the Financial Economic Crime Committee; the vendor of the TMX platform only provides the rules engine and has no role in setting or approving detection criteria.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: MDL-15 consists of three components that run daily after the end-of-day batch: (1) a scenario layer of 18 detection scenarios and three objective-indicator rules configured in the TMX platform, which generates alerts per customer; (2) a prioritisation layer, a LightGBM gradient-boosted classifier that estimates for every scenario alert the probability that it will be productive; and (3) a band assignment that maps the score to priority bands P1 to P5, of which P5 is the auto-closure band. Alerts generated for the same customer on the same day are grouped into one case for the analyst; the case inherits the highest priority band of its alerts. The prioritisation layer changes only the order of handling and, within the approved auto-closure band, the need for Level-1 review; it does not change which alerts are generated. The prioritisation layer uses the CRR class of MDL-16 as a feature and the thresholds of section 2.5 depend on it, so a CRR recalibration can shift the score distribution; MDL-16 changes are notified to the MDL-15 model owner and assessed before implementation (limitation L-TM-04). Conversely, MDL-16 uses only productive alerts and MOTs from MDL-15, not priority scores, to avoid circular amplification.

sections.heading: Changes in version 3.0
sections.text: Version 3.0 combines three related changes that are assessed as one change under CHG-2026-041: (a) the 2026 annual tuning of the scenario thresholds based on the ATL and BTL testing report EVD-15-ATL, including new scenario S18; (b) the replacement of the logistic regression prioritisation model of version 2.0 by a gradient-boosted model; and (c) the introduction of the auto-closure band P5. The combined impact at the most recent reference date (alerts of January–February 2027 rescored in the pre-production environment) is an increase of the generated alert volume by 3.6% from the threshold changes and a reduction of alerts routed to Level-1 review by 21.4% through the auto-closure band; 38.2% of alerts change priority band compared with version 2.0, which exceeds the 10% threshold of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e). The change is classified as internally material because it alters the methodology of the prioritisation layer, changes the range of use through auto-closure and exceeds the output-impact thresholds; the classification proposed by the developer was approved by Model Risk Management on 29 May 2026, and no regulatory class applies because the model does not require supervisory permission.

sections.heading: SIRA linkage and coverage matrix
sections.text: The design of the scenario catalogue follows the SIRA 2026, which Financial Crime Compliance drew up under the SIRA protocol FCC-PRT-001 and which was approved by the Financial Economic Crime Committee on 14 April 2026 and by the Management Board on 12 May 2026; the SIRA is performed annually and forms the basis for the transaction monitoring policy and this model. The SIRA 2026 identifies 24 material ML/TF risk scenarios based on risk factors relating to customers, products, services, transactions, delivery channels and geography, with likelihood and impact assessed per scenario, and takes into account the EU supranational risk assessment, the national risk assessment 2023 and FIU-Nederland typologies. Every material SIRA risk scenario is mapped in coverage matrix CM-TM-2026 version 3 to one or more detection controls: 21 risks are covered by one or more TM scenarios, two are covered by other controls (trade finance documentary checks and the correspondent banking monitoring model), and risk R-19 (misuse of accounts through third-party payment initiation services) is only partially covered and recorded as a gap with remediation plan RP-TM-2026-04, approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 3 June 2026 with target date 31 December 2027. The coverage matrix links SIRA risks to scenarios and documents coverage of customers, accounts, products and payment channels; the uncovered populations (institutional and correspondent banking customers, internal accounts and the Bank's own nostro accounts) are justified by coverage in other controls. The SIRA results, the coverage matrix and this documentation are kept up to date and are available to DNB on request; DNB received the SIRA 2026 and CM-TM-2026 in the thematic review of June 2026.

sections.heading: Segmentation and expected transaction profiles
sections.text: Customers are segmented into six behaviourally homogeneous segments, distinguishing natural persons, small businesses and corporates: RP-L retail low activity (1,412,600 customers, median monthly credit turnover below EUR 1,500), RP-M retail medium activity (1,021,300), RP-H retail high activity including private banking (184,500, above EUR 10,000), SB-1 sole proprietors (118,300), SB-2 small and medium-sized enterprises with turnover below EUR 10 million (88,600) and CO-1 corporates (7,500). The segmentation is supported statistically by a k-means analysis of twelve-month behavioural features (silhouette 0.41, Kruskal–Wallis tests on turnover and transaction count significant for all segment pairs) and was reviewed in the annual segment review of October 2026, which confirmed the boundaries (expert judgement EJ-TM-01). For every customer an expected transaction profile is derived from the CDD information (expected monthly turnover, expected cash use, expected countries) and from the customer's peer group within the segment, and scenarios S03, S11 and S13 compare conducted transactions with that profile to assess whether they are consistent with the Bank's knowledge of the customer.

sections.heading: Scenario library
sections.text: The scenario library in annex MDD-A gives for each of the 18 scenarios the objective, the typology addressed, the SIRA risk mapped, the customer, product and channel population, the specification, the segments and thresholds with their rationale, the exclusions, the pre-production test results and the tuning history since 2022; sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.3 summarise the scenarios by group. Together the scenarios address transactions that are complex, unusually large, conducted in an unusual pattern or without apparent economic or lawful purpose, so that the origin and destination of funds and the purpose of such transactions are examined by analysts. The scenario logic reflects the grounds for suspicion listed in the AMLR: customer and counterparty characteristics, transaction size, nature, methods and patterns, links between transactions, the origin and destination of funds and consistency with the customer's due diligence information and risk profile. Scenario exclusions are listed per scenario: the largest are the exclusion of transfers between accounts of the same customer from S05 and S08 (7.8% of the debit transaction volume) and the exclusion of salary and benefit payments from Dutch public bodies from S07 (4.1% of the credit transaction volume); both are justified by the absence of third-party layering risk.

sections.heading: Cash and rapid movement scenarios (S01–S08)
sections.text: S01 Large cash deposit alerts when cash deposits on one business day reach EUR 5,000 (RP-L), EUR 10,000 (RP-M, RP-H), EUR 15,000 (SB-1), EUR 25,000 (SB-2) or EUR 50,000 (CO-1). S02 Cash structuring alerts when a customer makes at least three cash deposits each between EUR 1,000 and EUR 9,999 with an aggregate of at least EUR 12,000 (retail segments) or EUR 20,000 (business segments) within a rolling look-back period of 10 calendar days, aggregated over all accounts of the customer and all deposit channels (branch, Geldmaat machines and business deposit service); deposits already alerted by S01 are excluded from the aggregate. S03 Cash intensity (SB-1, SB-2) alerts when the 90-day cash share of credit turnover is at least 60% and cash inflow is at least 2.5 times the expected cash inflow; S04 alerts on ATM withdrawals of at least EUR 2,500 within 30 days in countries of classes 4 and 5 of the Country Risk Matrix. In 2026 the cash group generated 31,900 alerts (19.6%) with a productive share of 11.2% and an MOT share of 5.0%. S05 Pass-through alerts when at least 80% of the 30-day credit turnover is debited within three business days and the credit turnover is at least EUR 15,000 (retail) or EUR 100,000 (business); S06 alerts on at least five outgoing round-amount transfers of at least EUR 5,000 within 30 days; S07 Funnel account alerts on at least 15 distinct remitters within 30 days with an aggregate of at least EUR 10,000 (RP-L, RP-M); S08 Dispersal alerts on at least 20 distinct beneficiaries within seven days with an aggregate of at least EUR 25,000. The rapid movement group generated 44,700 alerts (27.5%), productive share 12.4%, MOT share 5.6%.
