sections.heading: Geographic and profile deviation scenarios (S09–S13)
sections.text: S09 High-risk third countries alerts on any transfer of at least EUR 1,000 involving a counterparty or bank in a third country identified by the European Commission as high-risk under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675, so that the business relationships concerned are subject to enhanced monitoring; S10 alerts when the 30-day value of payments with countries of classes 4 and 5 of the Country Risk Matrix is at least three times the six-month average and at least EUR 10,000. The geographic scenarios use the Annex III higher-risk factors of the AML legislation, FIU-Nederland notifications on jurisdictions and the findings of the SIRA, all of which are reflected in the Country Risk Matrix maintained by Financial Crime Compliance; the group generated 22,100 alerts in 2026 (13.6%), productive share 6.3%, MOT share 2.4%. S11 Turnover deviation alerts when the 30-day credit turnover is at least 250% of the expected monthly turnover from the customer's CDD profile and exceeds the 99th percentile of the customer's peer group; for segment SB-2 the ratio was raised to 300% in the 2026 tuning (section 5.2). S12 Dormant account reactivation alerts when an account without customer-initiated transactions for at least twelve months receives at least EUR 10,000 within 30 days; S13 alerts when counterparties new to the customer account for at least 70% of the 30-day turnover and at least EUR 20,000. The profile deviation group generated 41,300 alerts (25.4%), productive share 7.1%, MOT share 2.7%, and is the main source of event-driven CDD reviews.

sections.heading: Typology scenarios (S14–S18) and Wwft objective indicators
sections.text: S14 Money-mule indicators alerts on accounts opened less than 180 days ago that receive at least eight incoming instant transfers from distinct private remitters within seven days, of which at least 80% of the value is forwarded or withdrawn within 48 hours; S15 alerts on crypto-asset service provider flows of at least EUR 15,000 within 30 days inconsistent with the profile or involving an unregistered provider; S16 alerts on international payments of SB-2 and CO-1 customers inconsistent with their SBI industry code; S17 alerts on repeated small transfers (cumulatively at least EUR 250 within 90 days) to beneficiaries on the FIU-Nederland typology list; S18, new in version 3.0 for SIRA risk R-11, alerts on early loan repayments of at least EUR 25,000 funded by cash or third parties. The typology group generated 22,400 alerts (13.8%), productive share 11.9%, MOT share 5.4%. The objective indicators of the Wwft Implementation Decree 2018 that apply to banks are implemented as three deterministic rules (OI-1 to OI-3) outside the prioritisation layer; a hit is by definition an unusual transaction and is routed directly to the FIU Reporting team. Reports to FIU-Nederland are made without delay once the unusual nature has become known, with the internal target of fourteen calendar days after the conclusion that a transaction is unusual; in 2026, 97.2% of the 6,658 MOTs arising from scenario alerts and all 1,214 objective-indicator reports met this target, and each report contained the prescribed data including the circumstances on which the transaction is deemed unusual. For every report the data needed to reconstruct the transaction, a copy of the report and the acknowledgement of FIU-Nederland are recorded retrievably in FCM-CM and retained for five years.

sections.heading: Risk-based monitoring intensity
sections.text: Monitoring is tailored to the risk class assigned by the Customer Risk Rating (MDL-16): for customers rated High, thresholds of scenarios S01, S02, S05, S10 and S11 are reduced by 40%, the look-back periods of S05 and S13 are extended to 60 days, and every alert on a High-risk customer is placed at least in priority band P2. Business relationships with politically exposed persons, their family members and close associates are subject to the same enhanced thresholds and, in addition, to scenario S13 at half the standard threshold, which implements the enhanced ongoing monitoring of PEP relationships. Customers rated Low, including customers to whom simplified due diligence is applied, remain subject to all scenarios at standard thresholds, so that simplified due diligence does not reduce transaction monitoring below the level needed to detect unusual transactions. When a scenario alert is found productive, the whole business relationship is subjected to enhanced monitoring for twelve months through the High-risk threshold set, irrespective of the CRR class.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is developed on the frozen reference data set RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1, documented in EVD-15-RDS version 1.0 approved on 19 March 2027, which contains 457,260 alerts generated between January 2024 and December 2026 with 43,512 productive alerts. The development, test and out-of-time samples were defined on 12 March 2027 before estimation: the out-of-time sample (158,850 alerts of 2026, productive rate 9.99%) was not used for variable selection, hyperparameter tuning or parameter estimation, and the development window (298,410 alerts of 2024–2025) was split into training (238,720 alerts) and test (59,690 alerts) samples grouped by customer. Objective-indicator hits (4,380 in the RDS, included in the counts above) are excluded from model estimation and performance measurement because they are not scored; the 1,420 randomly sampled low-priority alerts of 2026 are part of the out-of-time sample and are used to assess the auto-closure band without feedback-loop bias.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed for the prioritisation layer against documented criteria (performance, stability, interpretability, regulatory expectations, data requirements and implementation constraints): (1) re-estimation of the version 2.0 logistic regression with the extended feature set, (2) an explainable boosting machine (EBM) and (3) a LightGBM gradient-boosted model with monotone constraints. On the out-of-time sample the Gini coefficients were 0.602 (logistic regression), 0.651 (EBM) and 0.684 (LightGBM); LightGBM also achieved the lowest share of productive alerts in the auto-closure band at equal band size (0.8% compared with 1.9% for the logistic regression and 1.3% for the EBM). The less transparent LightGBM model was selected because its Gini uplift of 8.2 percentage points over the logistic regression and 3.3 percentage points over the EBM allows an auto-closure band within the 1% limit of FEC-STD-600 §8.4, which the transparent alternatives do not; the additional risks of the ML technique (opacity, overfitting and drift) are addressed by monotone constraints, stored local SHAP explanations with reason codes and monthly drift monitoring. For the scenario layer the rules-based approach was retained, because it is transparent to analysts and supervisors, directly traceable to SIRA risks and required to substantiate threshold values under the DNB guidance; an unsupervised anomaly detection layer was assessed in 2025 and rejected for insufficient explainability.

sections.heading: Scenario design and pre-production testing
sections.text: Scenarios are designed, calibrated, tested and tuned in accordance with FEC-STD-600: each new or changed scenario is specified by FEC Analytics, reviewed by Financial Crime Compliance and tested on historical data before production. Scenario S18 was tested on transactions of January 2024 – December 2026 before implementation: the expected alert volume is 95 alerts per month, it detects 23 of the 27 historical loan-repayment cases that were reported to FIU-Nederland after manual detection (85%), and its overlap with existing scenarios is 18% of alerts (mainly with S01). The changed scenarios S02, S06, S07, S11, S12 and S14 were tested in the same way, reporting for each the expected change in alert volume, the share of historically productive cases detected and the overlap with other scenarios; the results are recorded in annex MDD-A. Specifications are written precisely enough for independent re-implementation: Model Validation – Financial Crime re-implemented S02, S05 and S18 in Python for the 2026 periodic validation and the change validation.

sections.heading: Feature engineering and selection
sections.text: From 212 candidate features, each assessed for economic or behavioural rationale, availability at the alert timestamp in production and stability over the development window (PSI below 0.10 between 2024 and 2025), 64 features were retained for multivariate selection. Selection was performed on the training sample only: univariate AUC screening (minimum 0.52), removal of one of each pair of features with Spearman correlation above 0.85 (the feature with the clearer interpretation was kept), recursive elimination with grouped cross-validation, and removal of features with mean absolute SHAP below 1% of the total, which reduced the set to 46 features. Every engineered feature has an economic or behavioural interpretation, for example velocity_in_out_72h (share of credit value debited within 72 hours) for pass-through behaviour; no automatically generated features are used. All final drivers have a direction of effect consistent with expectations of Financial Crime Compliance, for example a higher threshold exceedance ratio, more prior productive alerts and a higher CRR class all increase the score; monotone constraints enforce the sign for eight features.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and hyperparameter tuning
sections.text: The prioritisation model is a binary LightGBM classifier (version 4.3.0) with binary log-loss objective; the hyperparameter search space (num_leaves 15–127, max_depth 3–10, learning_rate 0.01–0.2, min_child_samples 100–2,000, feature_fraction and bagging_fraction 0.5–1.0, lambda_l2 0–20) was searched with Bayesian optimisation (Optuna 3.6 TPE sampler, 200 trials) using five-fold cross-validation grouped by customer on the training sample, with mean cross-validated AUC as selection criterion; the test and out-of-time samples were never used for tuning. Overfitting is controlled by early stopping after 50 rounds without improvement on the validation fold (final 612 trees), a minimum of 400 alerts per leaf, a maximum depth of 6, L2 regularisation of 5.0, row and feature subsampling of 0.8 and monotone constraints on eight features. The final hyperparameters are num_leaves 31, max_depth 6, learning_rate 0.05, n_estimators 612, min_child_samples 400, feature_fraction 0.8, bagging_fraction 0.8 and lambda_l2 5.0. The scores are calibrated with isotonic regression on the test sample so that the score can be read as an estimated probability of a productive alert.

sections.heading: Threshold calibration
sections.text: Initial thresholds of each scenario are calibrated per segment on the statistical distribution of the scenario parameter over twelve months of transactions: the default is the 99.5th percentile of the parameter for retail segments and the 99th percentile for business segments, with the selected percentile and the expected monthly alert volume documented per scenario and segment in annex MDD-A. For S18 the threshold of EUR 25,000 corresponds to the 98.7th percentile of early repayments and an expected 95 alerts per month; the lower percentile was chosen because loan-back schemes are a SIRA risk rated high and the expected volume is small. Thresholds set or adjusted by expert judgement carry a documented risk-based rationale in the expert judgement log; operational capacity is not accepted as a rationale for raising a threshold, and the analyst capacity plan of Transaction Monitoring Operations is adjusted to the alert volume rather than the reverse. Threshold values are stored in the TMX platform parameter tables and band boundaries in the versioned scoring configuration of the prioritisation layer; both are changed only through change management.

sections.heading: Annual tuning based on ATL and BTL testing
sections.text: Every scenario was tuned in the 2026 cycle using the results of the above-the-line and below-the-line testing documented in EVD-15-ATL (report of 26 February 2027), which analysed alert outcomes above the thresholds and samples of non-alerted events in bands below them. As a result, the thresholds of S02, S06, S07 and S14 were lowered because BTL testing found productive events in the band directly below the threshold, and the thresholds of S11 for SB-2 (from 250% to 300% of expected turnover) and of S12 (from EUR 5,000 to EUR 10,000) were raised because ATL testing showed productive shares of 1.8% and 1.1% and BTL testing of the new bands found no productive events. The decisions not to change the thresholds of the other 11 scenarios are documented in EVD-15-ATL section 6 with the supporting ATL and BTL results. The tuning proposal was approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2027 and by the Financial Economic Crime Committee on 18 March 2027.

sections.heading: Priority bands and auto-closure band
sections.text: The calibrated score is mapped to five priority bands: P1 (score of at least 0.30), P2 (0.12 to below 0.30), P3 (0.05 to below 0.12), P4 (0.015 to below 0.05) and P5 (below 0.015); P1 to P4 determine only the order of Level-1 handling. P5 is proposed as an auto-closure band for alerts outside the excluded scenarios and customer groups. The share of productive alerts in the band on the out-of-time sample and the quality assurance arrangements will be added after the review of the random sample results.

sections.text: Not applicable: MDL-15 is not an IRB model and does not produce risk parameters to which a margin of conservatism under CRM-STD-101 applies; the heading is retained in accordance with MRM-STD-021 §2.2. Should monitoring show that the productive share in the auto-closure band approaches the 1% limit, the prescribed response is a reduction of the P5 boundary under change management, not an overlay.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power, calibration and stability were tested on the training, test and out-of-time samples with the metrics and thresholds of MV-HB-003: the AUC is 0.861 on the training sample (Gini 0.722), 0.851 on the test sample (Gini 0.702) and 0.842 on the out-of-time sample (Gini 0.684, 95% DeLong interval 0.676–0.692), and the calibration curve on the out-of-time sample lies within the 95% interval in nine of ten deciles (Hosmer–Lemeshow p-value 0.08). The Gini gap between the training and test samples is 2.0 percentage points and between training and out-of-time samples 3.8 percentage points, below the five-point threshold of AI-STD-700 §7.3. Measured out-of-time per scenario group, the AUC is 0.836 (cash), 0.861 (rapid movement), 0.812 (geography), 0.829 (profile deviation) and 0.803 (typology), and the recall of productive alerts by priority band is 41.2% in P1, 32.9% in P2, 18.6% in P3, 6.5% in P4 and 0.8% in P5. All results in chapter 7 were produced from estimation code tag tm-prio-v3.0.0 on RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1 (chapter 12).

sections.heading: Performance per segment
sections.text: Out-of-time performance was also measured for each segment: the AUC is 0.847 (RP-L), 0.838 (RP-M), 0.826 (RP-H), 0.831 (SB-1), 0.822 (SB-2) and 0.781 (CO-1). The CO-1 result is below the internal threshold of 0.80; the cause analysis attributes it to the small number of CO-1 alerts (3,900 in the RDS) and to the heterogeneity of corporate payment behaviour, the result is recorded as limitation L-TM-03 and the proposed mitigating measure is the exclusion of all CO-1 alerts from the auto-closure band until a dedicated corporate model is available. All other segment and scenario group results are above the internal threshold of 0.80 and show no significant calibration deviation.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and stability
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model the prioritisation layer is compared with a challenger: the logistic regression of version 2.0, re-estimated on the same data and target, reaches an out-of-time Gini of 0.602, so the LightGBM model provides an uplift of 8.2 percentage points, well above the two-point threshold of AI-STD-700 §10.3 below which the simpler model is preferred. The challenger does not outperform the selected model on any segment or scenario group and will be re-estimated annually and retained in the monitoring as a benchmark. Stability was demonstrated across time (quarterly out-of-time Gini between 0.671 and 0.697 in 2026), across segments (section 7.2) and across repeated training with five random seeds, where the standard deviation of the out-of-time Gini is 0.4 percentage points, below the one-point limit for Tier 1 models. The share of alerts in each priority band varied by less than 1.5 percentage points between the quarters of 2026, and the rank correlation of the SHAP importance of the top 20 features between the development and out-of-time samples is 0.93.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: alternative label definitions (MOT only as target: out-of-time Gini 0.662), the treatment of open alerts (all escalated open alerts treated as productive: change below 0.1 point), a 24-month instead of a 36-month window (Gini 0.677), the imputation of expected turnover (without imputation: minus 0.3 point) and the auto-closure boundary (0.010 to 0.020, productive share in P5 from 0.5% to 1.1%). The material expert judgements were also tested: using the unmapped disposition codes of the first half of 2024 as missing labels instead of the EJ-TM-06 mapping reduces the out-of-time Gini by 0.2 points, and removing the proxy-screened feature hrc_flow_share_90d (EJ-TM-07) reduces it by 1.1 points. The results confirm that the selected configuration is robust; the auto-closure boundary is the most sensitive parameter and is therefore monitored monthly (chapter 10).

sections.heading: Scenario effectiveness
sections.text: The technical functioning and effectiveness of the scenario layer are tested periodically: the annual ATL and BTL testing (EVD-15-ATL) tests effectiveness per scenario and segment, and the annual technical test of the TMX configuration (reconciliation of generated alerts against an independent Python re-implementation on a test data set) tests technical functioning. In 2026 the scenarios generated 162,400 alerts with a productive share of 9.9% and an MOT share of 4.1%, a false-positive share (non-productive alerts) of 90.1%; the productive share increased from 9.1% in 2024, and all 17 scenarios in production produced productive alerts in the last twelve months. The quality and effectiveness of the system are further demonstrated by the independent validations of Model Validation – Financial Crime (periodic validation of 9 October 2026, opinion Fit for purpose) and by the internal audit IA-2026-FEC-07.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the productive-alert label is a reasonable proxy for money-laundering relevance, supported by the 96.3% confirmation rate in the blind re-review of closed alerts; (A2) the relationship between features and productive outcomes is stable over at least one year, supported by the out-of-time results; (A3) CDD data used for expected profiles are sufficiently current, supported by the 97.8% CDD currency rate; and (A4) alerts from lowered thresholds behave like the lowest-scored alerts of the RDS, which is only weakly supported and therefore mitigated (L-TM-02). The intended use assumes that analysts review alerts in priority order within the service levels of Transaction Monitoring Operations; this assumption is monitored through the Level-1 service level indicator in chapter 10. Limitations are cross-referenced to the data deficiency log of EVD-15-RDS section 6.2 and to the expert judgement log in chapter 11.

sections.heading: Implementation and production controls
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-TM-3.0 version 1.1, approved by the model owner on 2 April 2027 before implementation started, is consistent with this MDD and defines for every input variable the production source field and lineage, every transformation, missing value and outlier treatment, the trained model artefact, the isotonic calibration table, the band boundaries and the auto-closure exclusion rules with precision and rounding conventions. The handover package to implementation of 6 April 2027 contains the implementation specification, the trained model artefact (model file lgbm_tm_v3.0.0.txt with SHA-256 hash), the feature caps and calibration tables, 1,250 test cases and reference outputs produced with the development code. The test cases cover typical alerts of every scenario group, segment and priority band, boundary values of the band boundaries, missing and invalid inputs and every auto-closure exclusion rule. The results of implementation testing, reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing are reported in EVD-15-IMPL. Production controls ensure that each daily run uses the approved model artefact and configuration version, verified by hash comparison at start-up, and every run is logged with reference date, input data version, code version and model version. The system automatically records every scoring event (alert identifier, feature vector, score, band, reason codes and SHAP values) in the scoring log, which is retained for five years together with the alert records. Production code and parameter tables (scoring configuration, band boundaries, feature caps and TMX threshold tables) are version controlled, access restricted and changed only through change management with four-eyes review by a person other than the author, and developers of FEC Analytics have no write access to the production environment. The model is not updated through continuous or online learning in production; retraining follows the approach of section 10.4.

sections.heading: Human oversight and alert handling
sections.text: Human oversight is designed as follows: Level-1 analysts of Transaction Monitoring Operations review every alert outside the auto-closure band, team leads monitor queue ageing and may re-prioritise cases with a documented reason, the Use Case Owner reviews the monthly oversight report, and the model owner can switch off the prioritisation layer (fallback to rule-based ordering by threshold exceedance) or the auto-closure band through a configuration flag with immediate effect. Level-1 review of each alert is completed within 30 calendar days of generation (96.8% compliance in 2026) and documented in FCM-CM so that the decision can be reconstructed, including the considerations and conclusion underlying each decision to close or escalate an alert and whether or not to report. A record of every assessment, including the information and circumstances considered, its result and, where applicable, a copy of the report to FIU-Nederland, is retained in FCM-CM whether or not a report was made. The model takes no decision to enter, refuse or maintain a business relationship or to change the extent of due diligence; productive alerts may lead to an event-driven CDD review or exit proposal, which is always decided by a CDD analyst or the Customer Integrity Committee, so that meaningful human intervention is ensured. Because the priority score does not play a determining role in a decision with legal or similarly significant effects on the customer, it is not treated as an automated individual decision under Art. 22 GDPR; this conclusion, including the assessment of the auto-closure band, which only results in no further action, is documented in DPIA-2024-031 with reference to the SCHUFA judgment. Analysts see the main drivers of each score and may escalate any alert irrespective of its priority, and the rate at which analysts escalate P4 alerts or close P1 alerts is monitored as the override indicator.

sections.heading: Transparency, instructions for use and AI literacy
sections.text: Customers can obtain an explanation of, and challenge, decisions on their relationship that follow from an event-driven review; however, no explanation is given of individual alerts or of their assessment, because these relate to the assessment under Art. 69 AMLR and to reports to FIU-Nederland, which are subject to the prohibition of disclosure. Instructions for use (TMO-GUI-011 version 3.0) describe for analysts and team leads the intended purpose of the priority score, the known limitations (in particular L-TM-01 to L-TM-03), the performance levels per band and the oversight tasks they are expected to perform, including the rule that a low score never justifies closing an alert without review outside the auto-closure band. Developers, validators, the Use Case Owner and all 214 analysts and team leads assigned to transaction monitoring complete the role-specific AI training module AI-LIT-TM before being assigned to the use case and a refresher every two years; completion was 100% for developers and validators and 97% for analysts on 31 May 2027, with the remaining analysts scheduled before go-live. The training covers the functioning of gradient boosting in plain language, the meaning and limits of reason codes, automation bias and the escalation route for suspected model errors.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan, KPIs and thresholds
sections.text: The monitoring plan of MDL-15 forms this chapter; it was approved by the model owner on 14 May 2027 and reviewed by Model Validation – Financial Crime as part of the change validation, and a red outcome triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation. The plan defines per KPI its calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments, responsible person and escalation: (a) out-of-time Gini on matured alerts, computed quarterly and compared with development (relative decline above 10% amber, above 20% red); (b) PSI of the score and of each of the 46 features against the development sample (amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25); (c) productive share in the auto-closure band estimated from the random sample (amber above 0.8%, red above 1.0% of productive alerts); (d) alert volume per scenario against the expected volume (amber ±25%, red ±50%); (e) productive and MOT share per scenario group; (f) Level-1 service level (amber below 95%, red below 90% within 30 days); (g) data feed reconciliation differences (amber above 0.1%, red above 0.5%); (h) fairness metrics; (i) override rates. All KPIs are computed for the whole model and for each segment and scenario group.

sections.heading: Drift, data and override monitoring
sections.text: Input drift is monitored monthly with the PSI of the score and of the ten most important features against the development sample, with amber above 0.10 and red above 0.25; the PSI of all 46 features is computed quarterly. The monitoring report shows model coverage, that is the share of generated alerts scored by the model (target 100% excluding objective-indicator hits) and the number of alerts with missing or outdated scores after fallback runs. Overrides in MDL-15 are re-prioritisations by team leads and deviations of analysts from the band order (closure of P1 alerts without escalation, escalation of P4 alerts); their rates are monitored monthly by direction, reason and team against the MRM-STD-023 §6.2 thresholds of 10% (amber) and 20% (red). The monitoring report presents override rates by direction, reason, magnitude (number of bands) and approving team, together with the realised productive rate of overridden compared with non-overridden alerts.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, MDL-15 is monitored at least quarterly, with operational KPIs reported monthly, and quarterly monitoring results are finalised and reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference quarter. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, and a root cause analysis with an action plan is submitted within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use (for example switching off the auto-closure band), with changes processed under MRM-STD-050. The quarterly monitoring report shows each KPI with its value, threshold, traffic light and trend over at least the last four monitoring cycles.

sections.heading: Retraining, tuning and annual review
sections.text: The retraining approach is defined as follows: the prioritisation model is retrained annually after the scenario tuning cycle on a rolling 36-month window, and additionally when triggered by a red Gini or score PSI result, a threshold change affecting more than 10% of alert volume or a new scenario; only the model parameters may change, within the approved feature set and hyperparameter search space. A retrained model must pass acceptance tests before use: out-of-time Gini of at least 0.64 and not more than two points below the production model, a productive share in the auto-closure band of at most 0.8%, fairness thresholds of AI-STD-700 §9.2 met, and a SHAP rank correlation of the top 20 features of at least 0.7; a retrained model outside these boundaries is treated as a material change. Every scenario is tuned at least annually and after material changes in products, customers, typologies or data, using the results of ATL and BTL testing. The model owner performs an annual model review covering monitoring results, portfolio and typology changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log, overlays and code-documentation consistency; the review concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the model owner and is submitted to Model Risk Management, and the monitoring plan is reviewed at the same time.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development of version 3.0 is described in this chapter with a reference to its entry in the expert judgement log EJL-MDL15, which is stored with the model documentation in DMS-FEC-MDL15 and is also referenced in the RDS documentation for judgements in data treatment; all judgements were documented and approved before the model outputs were used. The log records for each entry its type, life cycle stage and affected data, segment or parameter, the rationale, the evidence relied on and the alternatives rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver and date, and a review date with expiry conditions: EJ-TM-01 segment boundaries (design, low); EJ-TM-02 S11 threshold for SB-2 raised to 300% (calibration, medium); EJ-TM-03 S17 thresholds below the statistical percentile (calibration, medium); EJ-TM-04 auto-closure boundary 0.015 and exclusion rules (calibration, high); EJ-TM-05 choice of monotone constraints (design, low); EJ-TM-06 disposition code mapping 2024 (data treatment, medium); EJ-TM-07 retention of proxy-screened feature hrc_flow_share_90d (design, medium); EJ-TM-08 Country Risk Matrix mapping (data treatment, low); EJ-TM-09 S12 threshold raised to EUR 10,000 (calibration, low). For EJ-TM-04 the rationale states that a boundary of 0.015 keeps the productive share in the band at 0.8% while removing 21.4% of alerts from manual review, that boundaries of 0.020 and 0.010 were rejected (1.1% and 0.5% of productive alerts), and that the judgement expires if the monitored productive share exceeds 1.0% in two consecutive months; the rationale is specific enough for a third party to replicate its effect.

sections.heading: Materiality, challenge and approval
sections.text: Model Risk Management approved model-specific materiality thresholds for MDL-15 on 20 January 2027: an expert judgement is high materiality if it changes the volume of alerts routed to Level-1 review by more than 5% or the recall of productive alerts by more than 0.5 percentage point, medium above 1% or 0.2 point, and low otherwise; each judgement was classified against the output without the judgement or the best statistical alternative. Judgements whose impact cannot be quantified are classified as high materiality because MDL-15 is Tier 1. Approval follows materiality: low judgements by the model owner, medium judgements by the model owner and the Head of FEC Analytics Modelling, and the high judgement EJ-TM-04 by the MRC after review by Model Validation – Financial Crime; in no case is the proposer the sole approver. All medium and high judgements were challenged by a person independent of the proposer (Financial Crime Compliance for EJ-TM-02, EJ-TM-03 and EJ-TM-04, the AI Governance Office for EJ-TM-07, the Transaction Monitoring QA team for EJ-TM-06), and the challenge and its resolution are recorded in the log. The aggregate effect of all expert judgements is a reduction of the alert volume routed to Level-1 review by 21.9% and a reduction of productive recall by 0.9 percentage point compared with the statistical baseline, which exceeds the high materiality threshold and will therefore be submitted to the MRC together with the approval request.

sections.heading: Re-prioritisation rules and overlays
sections.text: Re-prioritisation of alerts by team leads is permitted only under procedure TMO-PRC-009, which specifies the permitted reasons (related open case, FIU or law-enforcement request, media report, customer contact), the maximum change (two bands, upwards without limit), the evidence required and the authority (team lead, senior team lead for downward changes). Each re-prioritisation is recorded in FCM-CM with a reason code, the supporting evidence and the approver. No overlays are applied in version 3.0; any future overlay must address a specific limitation, be quantified by a documented method and have a removal plan with target date.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This model development document (MDD) documents version 3.0 of MDL-15 AML Transaction Monitoring and follows the chapter structure, numbering and headings of the MDD template in Annex B to MRM-STD-021; chapter 6 is retained with the statement Not applicable. Cover block: title TM scenario and tuning documentation; model identifier MDL-15; model version 3.0; document version 1.0; status For validation; author S. Jansen (lead developer); reviewer R. Visser (senior developer, four-eyes review completed 12 May 2027); approvers M. Bakker (model owner) and P. de Graaf (Head of FEC Analytics Modelling); approval date 14 May 2027. The purpose of MDL-15 is to detect transactions and patterns of behaviour of retail and business payment customers that are unusual in relation to the customer's profile and risk, so that they can be assessed by analysts and, where the unusual nature is confirmed, reported to FIU-Nederland. The model monitors all transactions of the business relationship on an ongoing basis against the customer's due diligence information, expected transaction profile and risk class, and pays particular attention to unusual transaction patterns and to transaction types that by their nature carry a higher money-laundering or terrorist-financing risk, such as cash, rapid pass-through of funds and payments involving higher-risk jurisdictions. The intended use is the generation and prioritisation of alerts for Level-1 review; secondary uses are the provision of alert history as an input to the Customer Risk Rating (MDL-16) and to event-driven CDD reviews, and management information on scenario effectiveness for the SIRA. The model does not decide on reporting to FIU-Nederland, on exits or on account restrictions; those decisions are taken by analysts and by the FIU Reporting team.

sections.heading: Regulatory context
sections.text: The model is a key control for the Bank's obligations under Articles 2a, 3(2)(d), 8 and 16 of the Wwft and, from its date of application on 10 July 2027, Articles 26, 34 and 69 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), and it implements chapter 5 of the DNB Guidance on the Wwft and the Sanctions Act on transaction monitoring. Because the Bank's transaction volumes (on average 72 million transactions per month in 2026) do not permit manual monitoring, the Bank operates an automated monitoring system consisting of a substantiated set of detection scenarios with segment-specific threshold values, documented per scenario in section 2.4. Alerts are assessed against all relevant facts and information known to the Bank, and the Level-1 queue is ordered by the priority score so that the assessment of transactions with the highest risk is prioritised by urgency. The indicators of the Wwft Implementation Decree 2018 (Uitvoeringsbesluit Wwft 2018) for banks are implemented in full: the objective indicators are implemented as deterministic rules whose hits are reported without scoring (section 2.4.3), and the subjective indicator, grounds to suppose that a transaction may relate to money laundering or terrorist financing, underlies the scenario alerts and the analysts' assessment. The AMLR transition is tracked in project FEC-AMLR-2027; the scenario catalogue has been mapped to the AMLR provisions and no scenario change is required on the date of application, but the FIU-Nederland reporting format change is recorded as limitation L-TM-09.

sections.heading: AI Act assessment and AI Inventory
sections.text: The assessment against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act concludes that the scenario layer is not an AI system, because it applies fixed rules and thresholds defined by the Bank, whereas the prioritisation layer is an AI system, because it infers from alert, transaction and customer data how to generate predictions (priority scores) that influence the order of investigation. The use case is registered in the AI Inventory as AI-UC-2024-011, recording the purpose, the Use Case Owner and technical owner, the systems used, the Bank's role as provider and deployer, the affected persons (customers and counterparties), the data categories, the classifications and the Model Inventory identifier MDL-15. Under the AI Act the use case is classified as minimal risk: it is not a prohibited practice under Art. 5, AML transaction monitoring by a credit institution is not an Annex III use case, and customers do not interact directly with the system, so Art. 50 does not apply; the rationale was reviewed by the AI Governance Office on 24 February 2027. The internal AI Risk Class is Elevated, reflecting a Tier 1 model with material but indirect customer impact, human review of all alerts outside the auto-closure band and no automated customer decisions; the classification and AI Risk Class are reassessed at every material change, as for version 3.0, and at least annually. The system is not used for any practice prohibited by Art. 5 AI Act: it does not use manipulative techniques, does not exploit vulnerabilities and does not perform social scoring, because the score is used only within the AML process to order alerts and is never used to treat customers detrimentally in unrelated contexts.

sections.heading: Users, roles and lines of defence
sections.text: Transaction monitoring governance follows the three lines of defence: FEC Analytics (1LoD) develops and tunes the model, Transaction Monitoring Operations (1LoD) investigates alerts, Financial Crime Compliance (2LoD) approves coverage gaps, threshold rationales and BTL outcomes and decides on reports to FIU-Nederland, Model Validation – Financial Crime (2LoD) validates the model and Internal Audit (3LoD) audits the framework. The independent compliance function monitors the functioning of transaction monitoring and the timely reporting of unusual transactions to FIU-Nederland, and Internal Audit last audited transaction monitoring in audit IA-2026-FEC-07 (report of 30 September 2026, rating satisfactory with two medium findings, both closed). The model owner, M. Bakker, is the single accountable 1LoD senior manager recorded in the inventory and remains accountable for the tasks delegated to the TM Modelling team. The Bank has sufficient in-house understanding of the monitoring system: all scenario logic is specified, configured and tested by FEC Analytics, and the prioritisation model is developed in-house in Python; no vendor-supplied detection algorithm or vendor score is used. The criteria for the detection of unusual transactions, including scenario logic and thresholds, are approved by Financial Crime Compliance and the Financial Economic Crime Committee; the vendor of the TMX platform only provides the rules engine and has no role in setting or approving detection criteria.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: MDL-15 consists of three components that run daily after the end-of-day batch: (1) a scenario layer of 18 detection scenarios and three objective-indicator rules configured in the TMX platform, which generates alerts per customer; (2) a prioritisation layer, a LightGBM gradient-boosted classifier that estimates for every scenario alert the probability that it will be productive; and (3) a band assignment that maps the score to priority bands P1 to P5, of which P5 is the auto-closure band. Alerts generated for the same customer on the same day are grouped into one case for the analyst; the case inherits the highest priority band of its alerts. The prioritisation layer changes only the order of handling and, within the approved auto-closure band, the need for Level-1 review; it does not change which alerts are generated. The prioritisation layer uses the CRR class of MDL-16 as a feature and the thresholds of section 2.5 depend on it, so a CRR recalibration can shift the score distribution; MDL-16 changes are notified to the MDL-15 model owner and assessed before implementation (limitation L-TM-04). Conversely, MDL-16 uses only productive alerts and MOTs from MDL-15, not priority scores, to avoid circular amplification.

sections.heading: Changes in version 3.0
sections.text: Version 3.0 combines three related changes that are assessed as one change under CHG-2026-041: (a) the 2026 annual tuning of the scenario thresholds based on the ATL and BTL testing report EVD-15-ATL, including new scenario S18; (b) the replacement of the logistic regression prioritisation model of version 2.0 by a gradient-boosted model; and (c) the introduction of the auto-closure band P5. The combined impact at the most recent reference date (alerts of January–February 2027 rescored in the pre-production environment) is an increase of the generated alert volume by 3.6% from the threshold changes and a reduction of alerts routed to Level-1 review by 21.4% through the auto-closure band; 38.2% of alerts change priority band compared with version 2.0, which exceeds the 10% threshold of MRM-STD-050 §5.2(e). The change is classified as internally material because it alters the methodology of the prioritisation layer, changes the range of use through auto-closure and exceeds the output-impact thresholds; the classification proposed by the developer was approved by Model Risk Management on 29 May 2026, and no regulatory class applies because the model does not require supervisory permission.

sections.heading: SIRA linkage and coverage matrix
sections.text: The design of the scenario catalogue follows the SIRA 2026, which Financial Crime Compliance drew up under the SIRA protocol FCC-PRT-001 and which was approved by the Financial Economic Crime Committee on 14 April 2026 and by the Management Board on 12 May 2026; the SIRA is performed annually and forms the basis for the transaction monitoring policy and this model. The SIRA 2026 identifies 24 material ML/TF risk scenarios based on risk factors relating to customers, products, services, transactions, delivery channels and geography, with likelihood and impact assessed per scenario, and takes into account the EU supranational risk assessment, the national risk assessment 2023 and FIU-Nederland typologies. Every material SIRA risk scenario is mapped in coverage matrix CM-TM-2026 version 3 to one or more detection controls: 21 risks are covered by one or more TM scenarios, two are covered by other controls (trade finance documentary checks and the correspondent banking monitoring model), and risk R-19 (misuse of accounts through third-party payment initiation services) is only partially covered and recorded as a gap with remediation plan RP-TM-2026-04, approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 3 June 2026 with target date 31 December 2027. The coverage matrix links SIRA risks to scenarios and documents coverage of customers, accounts, products and payment channels; the uncovered populations (institutional and correspondent banking customers, internal accounts and the Bank's own nostro accounts) are justified by coverage in other controls. The SIRA results, the coverage matrix and this documentation are kept up to date and are available to DNB on request; DNB received the SIRA 2026 and CM-TM-2026 in the thematic review of June 2026.

sections.heading: Segmentation and expected transaction profiles
sections.text: Customers are segmented into six behaviourally homogeneous segments, distinguishing natural persons, small businesses and corporates: RP-L retail low activity (1,412,600 customers, median monthly credit turnover below EUR 1,500), RP-M retail medium activity (1,021,300), RP-H retail high activity including private banking (184,500, above EUR 10,000), SB-1 sole proprietors (118,300), SB-2 small and medium-sized enterprises with turnover below EUR 10 million (88,600) and CO-1 corporates (7,500). The segmentation is supported statistically by a k-means analysis of twelve-month behavioural features (silhouette 0.41, Kruskal–Wallis tests on turnover and transaction count significant for all segment pairs) and was reviewed in the annual segment review of October 2026, which confirmed the boundaries (expert judgement EJ-TM-01). For every customer an expected transaction profile is derived from the CDD information (expected monthly turnover, expected cash use, expected countries) and from the customer's peer group within the segment, and scenarios S03, S11 and S13 compare conducted transactions with that profile to assess whether they are consistent with the Bank's knowledge of the customer.

sections.heading: Scenario library
sections.text: The scenario library in annex MDD-A gives for each of the 18 scenarios the objective, the typology addressed, the SIRA risk mapped, the customer, product and channel population, the specification, the segments and thresholds with their rationale, the exclusions, the pre-production test results and the tuning history since 2022; sections 2.4.1 to 2.4.3 summarise the scenarios by group. Together the scenarios address transactions that are complex, unusually large, conducted in an unusual pattern or without apparent economic or lawful purpose, so that the origin and destination of funds and the purpose of such transactions are examined by analysts. The scenario logic reflects the grounds for suspicion listed in the AMLR: customer and counterparty characteristics, transaction size, nature, methods and patterns, links between transactions, the origin and destination of funds and consistency with the customer's due diligence information and risk profile. Scenario exclusions are listed per scenario: the largest are the exclusion of transfers between accounts of the same customer from S05 and S08 (7.8% of the debit transaction volume) and the exclusion of salary and benefit payments from Dutch public bodies from S07 (4.1% of the credit transaction volume); both are justified by the absence of third-party layering risk.

sections.heading: Cash and rapid movement scenarios (S01–S08)
sections.text: S01 Large cash deposit alerts when cash deposits on one business day reach EUR 5,000 (RP-L), EUR 10,000 (RP-M, RP-H), EUR 15,000 (SB-1), EUR 25,000 (SB-2) or EUR 50,000 (CO-1). S02 Cash structuring alerts when a customer makes at least three cash deposits each between EUR 1,000 and EUR 9,999 with an aggregate of at least EUR 12,000 (retail segments) or EUR 20,000 (business segments) within a rolling look-back period of 10 calendar days, aggregated over all accounts of the customer and all deposit channels (branch, Geldmaat machines and business deposit service); deposits already alerted by S01 are excluded from the aggregate. S03 Cash intensity (SB-1, SB-2) alerts when the 90-day cash share of credit turnover is at least 60% and cash inflow is at least 2.5 times the expected cash inflow; S04 alerts on ATM withdrawals of at least EUR 2,500 within 30 days in countries of classes 4 and 5 of the Country Risk Matrix. In 2026 the cash group generated 31,900 alerts (19.6%) with a productive share of 11.2% and an MOT share of 5.0%. S05 Pass-through alerts when at least 80% of the 30-day credit turnover is debited within three business days and the credit turnover is at least EUR 15,000 (retail) or EUR 100,000 (business); S06 alerts on at least five outgoing round-amount transfers of at least EUR 5,000 within 30 days; S07 Funnel account alerts on at least 15 distinct remitters within 30 days with an aggregate of at least EUR 10,000 (RP-L, RP-M); S08 Dispersal alerts on at least 20 distinct beneficiaries within seven days with an aggregate of at least EUR 25,000. The rapid movement group generated 44,700 alerts (27.5%), productive share 12.4%, MOT share 5.6%.

sections.heading: Geographic and profile deviation scenarios (S09–S13)
sections.text: S09 High-risk third countries alerts on any transfer of at least EUR 1,000 involving a counterparty or bank in a third country identified by the European Commission as high-risk under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/1675, so that the business relationships concerned are subject to enhanced monitoring; S10 alerts when the 30-day value of payments with countries of classes 4 and 5 of the Country Risk Matrix is at least three times the six-month average and at least EUR 10,000. The geographic scenarios use the Annex III higher-risk factors of the AML legislation, FIU-Nederland notifications on jurisdictions and the findings of the SIRA, all of which are reflected in the Country Risk Matrix maintained by Financial Crime Compliance; the group generated 22,100 alerts in 2026 (13.6%), productive share 6.3%, MOT share 2.4%. S11 Turnover deviation alerts when the 30-day credit turnover is at least 250% of the expected monthly turnover from the customer's CDD profile and exceeds the 99th percentile of the customer's peer group; for segment SB-2 the ratio was raised to 300% in the 2026 tuning (section 5.2). S12 Dormant account reactivation alerts when an account without customer-initiated transactions for at least twelve months receives at least EUR 10,000 within 30 days; S13 alerts when counterparties new to the customer account for at least 70% of the 30-day turnover and at least EUR 20,000. The profile deviation group generated 41,300 alerts (25.4%), productive share 7.1%, MOT share 2.7%, and is the main source of event-driven CDD reviews.

sections.heading: Typology scenarios (S14–S18) and Wwft objective indicators
sections.text: S14 Money-mule indicators alerts on accounts opened less than 180 days ago that receive at least eight incoming instant transfers from distinct private remitters within seven days, of which at least 80% of the value is forwarded or withdrawn within 48 hours; S15 alerts on crypto-asset service provider flows of at least EUR 15,000 within 30 days inconsistent with the profile or involving an unregistered provider; S16 alerts on international payments of SB-2 and CO-1 customers inconsistent with their SBI industry code; S17 alerts on repeated small transfers (cumulatively at least EUR 250 within 90 days) to beneficiaries on the FIU-Nederland typology list; S18, new in version 3.0 for SIRA risk R-11, alerts on early loan repayments of at least EUR 25,000 funded by cash or third parties. The typology group generated 22,400 alerts (13.8%), productive share 11.9%, MOT share 5.4%. The objective indicators of the Wwft Implementation Decree 2018 that apply to banks are implemented as three deterministic rules (OI-1 to OI-3) outside the prioritisation layer; a hit is by definition an unusual transaction and is routed directly to the FIU Reporting team. Reports to FIU-Nederland are made without delay once the unusual nature has become known, with the internal target of fourteen calendar days after the conclusion that a transaction is unusual; in 2026, 97.2% of the 6,658 MOTs arising from scenario alerts and all 1,214 objective-indicator reports met this target, and each report contained the prescribed data including the circumstances on which the transaction is deemed unusual. For every report the data needed to reconstruct the transaction, a copy of the report and the acknowledgement of FIU-Nederland are recorded retrievably in FCM-CM and retained for five years.

sections.heading: Risk-based monitoring intensity
sections.text: Monitoring is tailored to the risk class assigned by the Customer Risk Rating (MDL-16): for customers rated High, thresholds of scenarios S01, S02, S05, S10 and S11 are reduced by 40%, the look-back periods of S05 and S13 are extended to 60 days, and every alert on a High-risk customer is placed at least in priority band P2. Business relationships with politically exposed persons, their family members and close associates are subject to the same enhanced thresholds and, in addition, to scenario S13 at half the standard threshold, which implements the enhanced ongoing monitoring of PEP relationships. Customers rated Low, including customers to whom simplified due diligence is applied, remain subject to all scenarios at standard thresholds, so that simplified due diligence does not reduce transaction monitoring below the level needed to detect unusual transactions. When a scenario alert is found productive, the whole business relationship is subjected to enhanced monitoring for twelve months through the High-risk threshold set, irrespective of the CRR class.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is developed on the frozen reference data set RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1, documented in EVD-15-RDS version 1.0 approved on 19 March 2027, which contains 457,260 alerts generated between January 2024 and December 2026 with 43,512 productive alerts. The development, test and out-of-time samples were defined on 12 March 2027 before estimation: the out-of-time sample (158,850 alerts of 2026, productive rate 9.99%) was not used for variable selection, hyperparameter tuning or parameter estimation, and the development window (298,410 alerts of 2024–2025) was split into training (238,720 alerts) and test (59,690 alerts) samples grouped by customer. Objective-indicator hits (4,380 in the RDS, included in the counts above) are excluded from model estimation and performance measurement because they are not scored; the 1,420 randomly sampled low-priority alerts of 2026 are part of the out-of-time sample and are used to assess the auto-closure band without feedback-loop bias.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three methodologies were assessed for the prioritisation layer against documented criteria (performance, stability, interpretability, regulatory expectations, data requirements and implementation constraints): (1) re-estimation of the version 2.0 logistic regression with the extended feature set, (2) an explainable boosting machine (EBM) and (3) a LightGBM gradient-boosted model with monotone constraints. On the out-of-time sample the Gini coefficients were 0.602 (logistic regression), 0.651 (EBM) and 0.684 (LightGBM); LightGBM also achieved the lowest share of productive alerts in the auto-closure band at equal band size (0.8% compared with 1.9% for the logistic regression and 1.3% for the EBM). The less transparent LightGBM model was selected because its Gini uplift of 8.2 percentage points over the logistic regression and 3.3 percentage points over the EBM allows an auto-closure band within the 1% limit of FEC-STD-600 §8.4, which the transparent alternatives do not; the additional risks of the ML technique (opacity, overfitting and drift) are addressed by monotone constraints, stored local SHAP explanations with reason codes and monthly drift monitoring. For the scenario layer the rules-based approach was retained, because it is transparent to analysts and supervisors, directly traceable to SIRA risks and required to substantiate threshold values under the DNB guidance; an unsupervised anomaly detection layer was assessed in 2025 and rejected for insufficient explainability.

sections.heading: Scenario design and pre-production testing
sections.text: Scenarios are designed, calibrated, tested and tuned in accordance with FEC-STD-600: each new or changed scenario is specified by FEC Analytics, reviewed by Financial Crime Compliance and tested on historical data before production. Scenario S18 was tested on transactions of January 2024 – December 2026 before implementation: the expected alert volume is 95 alerts per month, it detects 23 of the 27 historical loan-repayment cases that were reported to FIU-Nederland after manual detection (85%), and its overlap with existing scenarios is 18% of alerts (mainly with S01). The changed scenarios S02, S06, S07, S11, S12 and S14 were tested in the same way, reporting for each the expected change in alert volume, the share of historically productive cases detected and the overlap with other scenarios; the results are recorded in annex MDD-A. Specifications are written precisely enough for independent re-implementation: Model Validation – Financial Crime re-implemented S02, S05 and S18 in Python for the 2026 periodic validation and the change validation.

sections.heading: Feature engineering and selection
sections.text: From 212 candidate features, each assessed for economic or behavioural rationale, availability at the alert timestamp in production and stability over the development window (PSI below 0.10 between 2024 and 2025), 64 features were retained for multivariate selection. Selection was performed on the training sample only: univariate AUC screening (minimum 0.52), removal of one of each pair of features with Spearman correlation above 0.85 (the feature with the clearer interpretation was kept), recursive elimination with grouped cross-validation, and removal of features with mean absolute SHAP below 1% of the total, which reduced the set to 46 features. Every engineered feature has an economic or behavioural interpretation, for example velocity_in_out_72h (share of credit value debited within 72 hours) for pass-through behaviour; no automatically generated features are used. All final drivers have a direction of effect consistent with expectations of Financial Crime Compliance, for example a higher threshold exceedance ratio, more prior productive alerts and a higher CRR class all increase the score; monotone constraints enforce the sign for eight features.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and hyperparameter tuning
sections.text: The prioritisation model is a binary LightGBM classifier (version 4.3.0) with binary log-loss objective; the hyperparameter search space (num_leaves 15–127, max_depth 3–10, learning_rate 0.01–0.2, min_child_samples 100–2,000, feature_fraction and bagging_fraction 0.5–1.0, lambda_l2 0–20) was searched with Bayesian optimisation (Optuna 3.6 TPE sampler, 200 trials) using five-fold cross-validation grouped by customer on the training sample, with mean cross-validated AUC as selection criterion; the test and out-of-time samples were never used for tuning. Overfitting is controlled by early stopping after 50 rounds without improvement on the validation fold (final 612 trees), a minimum of 400 alerts per leaf, a maximum depth of 6, L2 regularisation of 5.0, row and feature subsampling of 0.8 and monotone constraints on eight features. The final hyperparameters are num_leaves 31, max_depth 6, learning_rate 0.05, n_estimators 612, min_child_samples 400, feature_fraction 0.8, bagging_fraction 0.8 and lambda_l2 5.0. The scores are calibrated with isotonic regression on the test sample so that the score can be read as an estimated probability of a productive alert.

sections.heading: Threshold calibration
sections.text: Initial thresholds of each scenario are calibrated per segment on the statistical distribution of the scenario parameter over twelve months of transactions: the default is the 99.5th percentile of the parameter for retail segments and the 99th percentile for business segments, with the selected percentile and the expected monthly alert volume documented per scenario and segment in annex MDD-A. For S18 the threshold of EUR 25,000 corresponds to the 98.7th percentile of early repayments and an expected 95 alerts per month; the lower percentile was chosen because loan-back schemes are a SIRA risk rated high and the expected volume is small. Thresholds set or adjusted by expert judgement carry a documented risk-based rationale in the expert judgement log; operational capacity is not accepted as a rationale for raising a threshold, and the analyst capacity plan of Transaction Monitoring Operations is adjusted to the alert volume rather than the reverse. Threshold values are stored in the TMX platform parameter tables and band boundaries in the versioned scoring configuration of the prioritisation layer; both are changed only through change management.

sections.heading: Annual tuning based on ATL and BTL testing
sections.text: Every scenario was tuned in the 2026 cycle using the results of the above-the-line and below-the-line testing documented in EVD-15-ATL (report of 26 February 2027), which analysed alert outcomes above the thresholds and samples of non-alerted events in bands below them. As a result, the thresholds of S02, S06, S07 and S14 were lowered because BTL testing found productive events in the band directly below the threshold, and the thresholds of S11 for SB-2 (from 250% to 300% of expected turnover) and of S12 (from EUR 5,000 to EUR 10,000) were raised because ATL testing showed productive shares of 1.8% and 1.1% and BTL testing of the new bands found no productive events. The decisions not to change the thresholds of the other 11 scenarios are documented in EVD-15-ATL section 6 with the supporting ATL and BTL results. The tuning proposal was approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2027 and by the Financial Economic Crime Committee on 18 March 2027.

sections.heading: Priority bands and auto-closure band
sections.text: The calibrated score is mapped to five priority bands: P1 (score of at least 0.30), P2 (0.12 to below 0.30), P3 (0.05 to below 0.12), P4 (0.015 to below 0.05) and P5 (below 0.015); P1 to P4 determine only the order of Level-1 handling, with P1 alerts to be reviewed within five business days. P5 is an auto-closure band: alerts in P5 are closed by the model without Level-1 review, except alerts from S09, S17 and S18, alerts from thresholds lowered in version 3.0, alerts on customers rated High, PEPs, customers with an MOT in the previous 24 months and all alerts of segment CO-1, which are placed in P4 regardless of score. In the out-of-time sample the P5 band contains 21.4% of all alerts and 0.8% of the productive alerts (127 of 15,872), within the limit of 1% of FEC-STD-600 §8.4; each month at least 60 auto-closed alerts are reviewed by the Transaction Monitoring QA team in addition to the 2% random sample of P4 and P5 alerts. The auto-closure logic was approved by the Financial Economic Crime Committee on 22 April 2027, conditional on the validation of version 3.0 by Model Validation – Financial Crime and on the approval of the model by the MRC, and is subject to the monthly sample-based quality assurance described above.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power, calibration and stability were tested on the training, test and out-of-time samples with the metrics and thresholds of MV-HB-003: the AUC is 0.861 on the training sample (Gini 0.722), 0.851 on the test sample (Gini 0.702) and 0.842 on the out-of-time sample (Gini 0.684, 95% DeLong interval 0.676–0.692), and the calibration curve on the out-of-time sample lies within the 95% interval in nine of ten deciles (Hosmer–Lemeshow p-value 0.08). The Gini gap between the training and test samples is 2.0 percentage points and between training and out-of-time samples 3.8 percentage points, below the five-point threshold of AI-STD-700 §7.3. Measured out-of-time per scenario group, the AUC is 0.836 (cash), 0.861 (rapid movement), 0.812 (geography), 0.829 (profile deviation) and 0.803 (typology), and the recall of productive alerts by priority band is 41.2% in P1, 32.9% in P2, 18.6% in P3, 6.5% in P4 and 0.8% in P5. All results in chapter 7 were produced from estimation code tag tm-prio-v3.0.0 on RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1 (chapter 12).

sections.heading: Performance per segment
sections.text: Out-of-time performance was also measured for each segment: the AUC is 0.847 (RP-L), 0.838 (RP-M), 0.826 (RP-H), 0.831 (SB-1), 0.822 (SB-2) and 0.781 (CO-1). The CO-1 result is below the internal threshold of 0.80; the cause analysis attributes it to the small number of CO-1 alerts (3,900 in the RDS) and to the heterogeneity of corporate payment behaviour, the result is recorded as limitation L-TM-03 and the proposed mitigating measure is the exclusion of all CO-1 alerts from the auto-closure band until a dedicated corporate model is available. All other segment and scenario group results are above the internal threshold of 0.80 and show no significant calibration deviation.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and stability
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model the prioritisation layer is compared with a challenger: the logistic regression of version 2.0, re-estimated on the same data and target, reaches an out-of-time Gini of 0.602, so the LightGBM model provides an uplift of 8.2 percentage points, well above the two-point threshold of AI-STD-700 §10.3 below which the simpler model is preferred. The challenger does not outperform the selected model on any segment or scenario group and will be re-estimated annually and retained in the monitoring as a benchmark. Stability was demonstrated across time (quarterly out-of-time Gini between 0.671 and 0.697 in 2026), across segments (section 7.2) and across repeated training with five random seeds, where the standard deviation of the out-of-time Gini is 0.4 percentage points, below the one-point limit for Tier 1 models. The share of alerts in each priority band varied by less than 1.5 percentage points between the quarters of 2026, and the rank correlation of the SHAP importance of the top 20 features between the development and out-of-time samples is 0.93.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: alternative label definitions (MOT only as target: out-of-time Gini 0.662), the treatment of open alerts (all escalated open alerts treated as productive: change below 0.1 point), a 24-month instead of a 36-month window (Gini 0.677), the imputation of expected turnover (without imputation: minus 0.3 point) and the auto-closure boundary (0.010 to 0.020, productive share in P5 from 0.5% to 1.1%). The material expert judgements were also tested: using the unmapped disposition codes of the first half of 2024 as missing labels instead of the EJ-TM-06 mapping reduces the out-of-time Gini by 0.2 points, and removing the proxy-screened feature hrc_flow_share_90d (EJ-TM-07) reduces it by 1.1 points. The results confirm that the selected configuration is robust; the auto-closure boundary is the most sensitive parameter and is therefore monitored monthly (chapter 10).

sections.heading: Explainability, fairness and robustness
sections.text: In accordance with AI-STD-700 and MRM-STD-021 §5.8, this section summarises the explainability, fairness and robustness analyses documented in detail in EVD-15-XAI version 1.0. The main global drivers by mean absolute SHAP value are the threshold exceedance ratio (14.8%), prior productive alerts in 24 months (11.2%), the CRR class (8.9%), the cash share of inflows (7.4%) and the share of flows with higher-risk countries (6.1%), consistent with the expectations of Financial Crime Compliance; for every scored alert the local SHAP values and the three highest-ranked reason codes are stored and displayed to the analyst. Fairness was tested before approval for sex, age group and nationality group: the lowest adverse-impact ratio is 0.84 (age group 18–29 compared with 45–64) and the largest difference in true-positive rates is 4.1 percentage points (age groups), both within the thresholds of AI-STD-700 §9.2; fairness will be monitored quarterly during use. Robustness tests show that perturbations of ±5% of continuous inputs change the priority band of 2.3% of alerts, that missing and extreme values are handled as specified, and that simulated evasion (splitting cash deposits to stay below S02) reduces detection by S02 but is partly compensated by S01 and S03; cyber risks (data poisoning, model extraction) were assessed with Information Security in assessment ISA-2027-031.

sections.heading: Scenario effectiveness
sections.text: The technical functioning and effectiveness of the scenario layer are tested periodically: the annual ATL and BTL testing (EVD-15-ATL) tests effectiveness per scenario and segment, and the annual technical test of the TMX configuration (reconciliation of generated alerts against an independent Python re-implementation on a test data set) tests technical functioning. In 2026 the scenarios generated 162,400 alerts with a productive share of 9.9% and an MOT share of 4.1%, a false-positive share (non-productive alerts) of 90.1%; the productive share increased from 9.1% in 2024, and all 17 scenarios in production produced productive alerts in the last twelve months. The quality and effectiveness of the system are further demonstrated by the independent validations of Model Validation – Financial Crime (periodic validation of 9 October 2026, opinion Fit for purpose) and by the internal audit IA-2026-FEC-07.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (A1) the productive-alert label is a reasonable proxy for money-laundering relevance, supported by the 96.3% confirmation rate in the blind re-review of closed alerts; (A2) the relationship between features and productive outcomes is stable over at least one year, supported by the out-of-time results; (A3) CDD data used for expected profiles are sufficiently current, supported by the 97.8% CDD currency rate; and (A4) alerts from lowered thresholds behave like the lowest-scored alerts of the RDS, which is only weakly supported and therefore mitigated (L-TM-02). The intended use assumes that analysts review alerts in priority order within the service levels of Transaction Monitoring Operations; this assumption is monitored through the Level-1 service level indicator in chapter 10. Limitations are cross-referenced to the data deficiency log of EVD-15-RDS section 6.2 and to the expert judgement log in chapter 11.

sections.heading: Implementation and production controls
sections.text: The implementation specification IS-TM-3.0 version 1.1, approved by the model owner on 2 April 2027 before implementation started, is consistent with this MDD and defines for every input variable the production source field and lineage, every transformation, missing value and outlier treatment, the trained model artefact, the isotonic calibration table, the band boundaries and the auto-closure exclusion rules with precision and rounding conventions. The handover package to implementation of 6 April 2027 contains the implementation specification, the trained model artefact (model file lgbm_tm_v3.0.0.txt with SHA-256 hash), the feature caps and calibration tables, 1,250 test cases and reference outputs produced with the development code. The test cases cover typical alerts of every scenario group, segment and priority band, boundary values of the band boundaries, missing and invalid inputs and every auto-closure exclusion rule. The results of implementation testing, reconciliation, the parallel run and user acceptance testing are reported in EVD-15-IMPL. Production controls ensure that each daily run uses the approved model artefact and configuration version, verified by hash comparison at start-up, and every run is logged with reference date, input data version, code version and model version. The system automatically records every scoring event (alert identifier, feature vector, score, band, reason codes and SHAP values) in the scoring log, which is retained for five years together with the alert records. Production code and parameter tables (scoring configuration, band boundaries, feature caps and TMX threshold tables) are version controlled, access restricted and changed only through change management with four-eyes review by a person other than the author, and developers of FEC Analytics have no write access to the production environment. The model is not updated through continuous or online learning in production; retraining follows the approach of section 10.4.

sections.heading: Human oversight and alert handling
sections.text: Human oversight is designed as follows: Level-1 analysts of Transaction Monitoring Operations review every alert outside the auto-closure band, team leads monitor queue ageing and may re-prioritise cases with a documented reason, the Use Case Owner reviews the monthly oversight report, and the model owner can switch off the prioritisation layer (fallback to rule-based ordering by threshold exceedance) or the auto-closure band through a configuration flag with immediate effect. Level-1 review of each alert is completed within 30 calendar days of generation (96.8% compliance in 2026) and documented in FCM-CM so that the decision can be reconstructed, including the considerations and conclusion underlying each decision to close or escalate an alert and whether or not to report. A record of every assessment, including the information and circumstances considered, its result and, where applicable, a copy of the report to FIU-Nederland, is retained in FCM-CM whether or not a report was made. The model takes no decision to enter, refuse or maintain a business relationship or to change the extent of due diligence; productive alerts may lead to an event-driven CDD review or exit proposal, which is always decided by a CDD analyst or the Customer Integrity Committee, so that meaningful human intervention is ensured. Because the priority score does not play a determining role in a decision with legal or similarly significant effects on the customer, it is not treated as an automated individual decision under Art. 22 GDPR; this conclusion, including the assessment of the auto-closure band, which only results in no further action, is documented in DPIA-2024-031 with reference to the SCHUFA judgment. Analysts see the main drivers of each score and may escalate any alert irrespective of its priority, and the rate at which analysts escalate P4 alerts or close P1 alerts is monitored as the override indicator.

sections.heading: Transparency, instructions for use and AI literacy
sections.text: Customers can obtain an explanation of, and challenge, decisions on their relationship that follow from an event-driven review; however, no explanation is given of individual alerts or of their assessment, because these relate to the assessment under Art. 69 AMLR and to reports to FIU-Nederland, which are subject to the prohibition of disclosure. Instructions for use (TMO-GUI-011 version 3.0) describe for analysts and team leads the intended purpose of the priority score, the known limitations (in particular L-TM-01 to L-TM-03), the performance levels per band and the oversight tasks they are expected to perform, including the rule that a low score never justifies closing an alert without review outside the auto-closure band. Developers, validators, the Use Case Owner and all 214 analysts and team leads assigned to transaction monitoring complete the role-specific AI training module AI-LIT-TM before being assigned to the use case and a refresher every two years; completion was 100% for developers and validators and 97% for analysts on 31 May 2027, with the remaining analysts scheduled before go-live. The training covers the functioning of gradient boosting in plain language, the meaning and limits of reason codes, automation bias and the escalation route for suspected model errors.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan, KPIs and thresholds
sections.text: The monitoring plan of MDL-15 forms this chapter; it was approved by the model owner on 14 May 2027 and reviewed by Model Validation – Financial Crime as part of the change validation, and a red outcome triggers a review by the model owner and notification of Model Risk Management and Model Validation. The plan defines per KPI its calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments, responsible person and escalation: (a) out-of-time Gini on matured alerts, computed quarterly and compared with development (relative decline above 10% amber, above 20% red); (b) PSI of the score and of each of the 46 features against the development sample (amber 0.10–0.25, red above 0.25); (c) productive share in the auto-closure band estimated from the random sample (amber above 0.8%, red above 1.0% of productive alerts); (d) alert volume per scenario against the expected volume (amber ±25%, red ±50%); (e) productive and MOT share per scenario group; (f) Level-1 service level (amber below 95%, red below 90% within 30 days); (g) data feed reconciliation differences (amber above 0.1%, red above 0.5%); (h) fairness metrics; (i) override rates. All KPIs are computed for the whole model and for each segment and scenario group.

sections.heading: Drift, data and override monitoring
sections.text: Input drift is monitored monthly with the PSI of the score and of the ten most important features against the development sample, with amber above 0.10 and red above 0.25; the PSI of all 46 features is computed quarterly. The monitoring report shows model coverage, that is the share of generated alerts scored by the model (target 100% excluding objective-indicator hits) and the number of alerts with missing or outdated scores after fallback runs. Overrides in MDL-15 are re-prioritisations by team leads and deviations of analysts from the band order (closure of P1 alerts without escalation, escalation of P4 alerts); their rates are monitored monthly by direction, reason and team against the MRM-STD-023 §6.2 thresholds of 10% (amber) and 20% (red). The monitoring report presents override rates by direction, reason, magnitude (number of bands) and approving team, together with the realised productive rate of overridden compared with non-overridden alerts.
