sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, MDL-15 is monitored at least quarterly, with operational KPIs reported monthly, and quarterly monitoring results are finalised and reported within 60 calendar days after the end of the reference quarter. Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, and a root cause analysis with an action plan is submitted within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use (for example switching off the auto-closure band), with changes processed under MRM-STD-050. The quarterly monitoring report shows each KPI with its value, threshold, traffic light and trend over at least the last four monitoring cycles.

sections.heading: Retraining, tuning and annual review
sections.text: The retraining approach is defined as follows: the prioritisation model is retrained annually after the scenario tuning cycle on a rolling 36-month window, and additionally when triggered by a red Gini or score PSI result, a threshold change affecting more than 10% of alert volume or a new scenario; only the model parameters may change, within the approved feature set and hyperparameter search space. A retrained model must pass acceptance tests before use: out-of-time Gini of at least 0.64 and not more than two points below the production model, a productive share in the auto-closure band of at most 0.8%, fairness thresholds of AI-STD-700 §9.2 met, and a SHAP rank correlation of the top 20 features of at least 0.7; a retrained model outside these boundaries is treated as a material change. Every scenario is tuned at least annually and after material changes in products, customers, typologies or data, using the results of ATL and BTL testing. The model owner performs an annual model review covering monitoring results, portfolio and typology changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log, overlays and code-documentation consistency; the review concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose, is signed off by the model owner and is submitted to Model Risk Management, and the monitoring plan is reviewed at the same time.

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development of version 3.0 is described in this chapter with a reference to its entry in the expert judgement log EJL-MDL15, which is stored with the model documentation in DMS-FEC-MDL15 and is also referenced in the RDS documentation for judgements in data treatment; all judgements were documented and approved before the model outputs were used. The log records for each entry its type, life cycle stage and affected data, segment or parameter, the rationale, the evidence relied on and the alternatives rejected, the quantified impact, the proposer, the approver and date, and a review date with expiry conditions: EJ-TM-01 segment boundaries (design, low); EJ-TM-02 S11 threshold for SB-2 raised to 300% (calibration, medium); EJ-TM-03 S17 thresholds below the statistical percentile (calibration, medium); EJ-TM-04 auto-closure boundary 0.015 and exclusion rules (calibration, high); EJ-TM-05 choice of monotone constraints (design, low); EJ-TM-06 disposition code mapping 2024 (data treatment, medium); EJ-TM-07 retention of proxy-screened feature hrc_flow_share_90d (design, medium); EJ-TM-08 Country Risk Matrix mapping (data treatment, low); EJ-TM-09 S12 threshold raised to EUR 10,000 (calibration, low). For EJ-TM-04 the rationale states that a boundary of 0.015 keeps the productive share in the band at 0.8% while removing 21.4% of alerts from manual review, that boundaries of 0.020 and 0.010 were rejected (1.1% and 0.5% of productive alerts), and that the judgement expires if the monitored productive share exceeds 1.0% in two consecutive months; the rationale is specific enough for a third party to replicate its effect.

sections.heading: Materiality, challenge and approval
sections.text: Model Risk Management approved model-specific materiality thresholds for MDL-15 on 20 January 2027: an expert judgement is high materiality if it changes the volume of alerts routed to Level-1 review by more than 5% or the recall of productive alerts by more than 0.5 percentage point, medium above 1% or 0.2 point, and low otherwise; each judgement was classified against the output without the judgement or the best statistical alternative. Judgements whose impact cannot be quantified are classified as high materiality because MDL-15 is Tier 1. Approval follows materiality: low judgements by the model owner, medium judgements by the model owner and the Head of FEC Analytics Modelling, and the high judgement EJ-TM-04 by the MRC after review by Model Validation – Financial Crime; in no case is the proposer the sole approver. All medium and high judgements were challenged by a person independent of the proposer (Financial Crime Compliance for EJ-TM-02, EJ-TM-03 and EJ-TM-04, the AI Governance Office for EJ-TM-07, the Transaction Monitoring QA team for EJ-TM-06), and the challenge and its resolution are recorded in the log. The aggregate effect of all expert judgements is a reduction of the alert volume routed to Level-1 review by 21.9% and a reduction of productive recall by 0.9 percentage point compared with the statistical baseline, which exceeds the high materiality threshold and will therefore be submitted to the MRC together with the approval request.

sections.heading: Re-prioritisation rules and overlays
sections.text: Re-prioritisation of alerts by team leads is permitted only under procedure TMO-PRC-009, which specifies the permitted reasons (related open case, FIU or law-enforcement request, media report, customer contact), the maximum change (two bands, upwards without limit), the evidence required and the authority (team lead, senior team lead for downward changes). Each re-prioritisation is recorded in FCM-CM with a reason code, the supporting evidence and the approver. No overlays are applied in version 3.0; any future overlay must address a specific limitation, be quantified by a documented method and have a removal plan with target date.

sections.heading: Reproducibility and code review
sections.text: The software environment is recorded in the lock file environment-model.lock (Python 3.11.8, lightgbm 4.3.0, optuna 3.6.1, shap 0.45.0, scikit-learn 1.4.1) with fixed random seed 20270315, and the full pipeline from RDS to band assignment is executable with one command, so that Model Validation can reproduce every result. The development code was reviewed by R. Visser, who did not write it, before the results were submitted to Model Validation (merge requests !412 to !447, review completed 9 May 2027). The RDS documentation, this MDD, the implementation specification IS-TM-3.0 and the production code are consistent; the consistency check of 12 May 2027 compared the parameters of the prioritisation layer (feature caps, calibration table, band boundaries and auto-closure exclusion rules) with the production scoring configuration, while the TMX scenario parameters are covered by the implementation testing reported in EVD-15-IMPL.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report documents the above-the-line (ATL) and below-the-line (BTL) testing of the transaction monitoring scenarios of MDL-15 performed in the 2026 annual testing cycle, and the resulting proposals for threshold changes implemented in model version 3.0. ATL testing covers all 17 scenarios in production in 2026 and all segments; BTL testing covers all 17 threshold-based scenarios, with scenario S18 tested before production as documented in the MDD section 4.2. The testing was performed by FEC Analytics between 1 October 2026 and 31 January 2027 on alerts generated from 1 January to 31 December 2026 and on below-the-line events generated from transactions of July to December 2026. Report version 1.0 of 26 February 2027; author L. Hendriks (FEC Analytics); reviewer S. Jansen; approved by M. Bakker (model owner) and, for the threshold rationales and BTL outcomes, by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2027.

sections.heading: ATL methodology
sections.text: ATL testing reports for every scenario and segment the alert volume, the share of productive alerts (escalated to Level-2 investigation or contributing to a report), the share of alerts resulting in a report to FIU-Nederland and the quality of the disposition of closed non-productive alerts, based on a quality-assurance sample. The QA sample consists of 400 closed non-productive alerts drawn by stratified random sampling (25 per scenario for the 16 scenarios with at least 1,000 non-productive alerts, and all eligible alerts of S17) and re-reviewed by the Transaction Monitoring QA team against the documentation standard of TMO-PRC-004. Productive and report shares are compared with the previous two cycles, and scenarios with a productive share below 2% in any segment are flagged for review of the threshold or the scenario design.

sections.heading: BTL methodology
sections.text: For each threshold-based scenario, test events are generated by re-running the scenario in the TMX test environment with lowered thresholds and retaining the events that fall below the production threshold, in two bands: band 1 from the threshold down to 10% below it and band 2 from 10% to 20% below it; where band 1 contained productive events, a third band down to 30% below the threshold was added. Per band a simple random sample of 60 events is reviewed, which exceeds the minimum of 59 events at which the absence of productive events supports a productive rate below 5% at 95% confidence; where a band contained fewer than 60 events all events were reviewed. The events were reviewed by twelve trained Level-1 analysts of Transaction Monitoring Operations, blind to the fact that they were test events: the events were loaded into the regular alert queue of FCM-CM with the standard alert layout and were dispositioned under the normal procedure, with escalated events handled by the Level-2 team. In total 2,220 BTL events were reviewed: 17 scenarios with two bands of 60 events and three additional third bands (S02, S07 and S14).

sections.heading: ATL results
sections.text: In 2026 the 17 scenarios generated 162,400 alerts, of which 16,106 (9.9%) were productive and 6,658 (4.1%) resulted in an MOT, against 9.4% and 3.9% in 2025; by scenario group the productive shares were cash 11.2%, rapid movement 12.4%, geography 6.3%, profile deviation 7.1% and typology 11.9%, and the MOT shares 5.0%, 5.6%, 2.4%, 2.7% and 5.4%. The highest productive shares were observed for S14 money-mule indicators (18.3%) and S05 pass-through (14.9%), the lowest for S12 dormant account reactivation (1.1%) and S11 turnover deviation in segment SB-2 (1.8%). By segment the productive shares were RP-L 10.8%, RP-M 9.1%, RP-H 11.3%, SB-1 9.6%, SB-2 7.4% and CO-1 8.2%. Alert volumes per scenario deviated by less than 15% from the expected volumes set in the 2025 cycle, except for S14 (+31%), which reflects the growth of money-mule activity reported by FIU-Nederland.

sections.heading: BTL results and threshold decisions
sections.text: Productive events were found below the thresholds of four scenarios: S02 cash structuring (band 1: 4 of 60, band 2: 1 of 60, band 3: 0 of 60), S07 funnel account (band 1: 3 of 60, bands 2 and 3: 0), S14 money-mule indicators (band 1: 5 of 60, band 2: 2 of 60, band 3: 0 of 60) and S06 round-amount transfers (band 1: 2 of 60). In each case the threshold is lowered to capture the productive events: S02 aggregate from EUR 15,000 to EUR 12,000 for retail segments, S07 from 20 to 15 distinct remitters, S14 from ten to eight incoming instant transfers and S06 from EUR 7,500 to EUR 5,000 per transfer; the expected additional alert volume is 520 alerts per month. For the other 13 scenarios no productive events were found in any band; the thresholds of 11 of them remain unchanged, and these decisions are documented per scenario with the ATL and BTL results in annex ATL-B, while the two increases are set out in section 6.1.

sections.heading: Threshold increases
sections.text: Two thresholds are raised: S12 dormant account reactivation from EUR 5,000 to EUR 10,000, because only 1.1% of its alerts in the band from EUR 5,000 to EUR 10,000 were productive and none of those resulted in an MOT, and S11 turnover deviation for segment SB-2 from 250% to 300% of expected turnover, because the productive share of SB-2 alerts between 250% and 300% was 1.8% in 2026 and no MOT resulted from that band. The increase of the S11 threshold for SB-2 also reduces the SB-2 alert backlog of Transaction Monitoring Operations by around 380 alerts per month, which allows analysts to focus on higher-risk SB-2 alerts. After both increases, BTL testing of the newly created bands below the new thresholds (two bands of 60 events each per scenario) found no productive events, and the increases were approved by Financial Crime Compliance on 4 March 2027 as expert judgements EJ-TM-02 and EJ-TM-09.

sections.heading: Disposition quality
sections.text: Of the 400 closed non-productive alerts in the QA sample, 378 (94.5%) were correctly dispositioned and adequately documented, 13 (3.2%) were correctly closed but with insufficient documentation of the considerations, and 9 (2.3%) should have been escalated; the nine alerts were reopened, and three of them resulted in an MOT. The documentation shortcomings concentrate in S11 and S13 alerts on business customers, where analysts did not always record why the deviation from the expected profile was explained. Transaction Monitoring Operations has added a mandatory explanation field for profile deviation alerts (change TMO-CR-2027-006, implemented on 15 February 2027).

sections.heading: Scenario effectiveness conclusions
sections.text: The testing shows that the scenario set is effective overall: all 17 scenarios produced productive alerts in 2026, the productive share increased for the third consecutive year, and the BTL results led to targeted threshold reductions for the scenarios where relevant activity was being missed. The threshold settings resulting from this cycle are substantiated by the ATL and BTL analyses in this report, which forms the basis for the thresholds of model version 3.0 documented in MDD section 5.2. The low productive share of geography scenarios is explained by the high share of legitimate family remittances among S09 alerts; the scenario remains necessary because the enhanced monitoring of links with high-risk third countries is a legal requirement.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report documents the explainability, fairness and robustness analyses of the prioritisation layer of MDL-15 version 3.0 required by AI-STD-700 and summarised in section 7.5 of the MDD; it covers hyperparameter and overfitting controls only by reference to MDD section 4.4. All analyses were performed on the test and out-of-time samples of RDS-TM-ALERT-2027.1 with code tag tm-prio-v3.0.0 and the shap library version 0.45.0 (TreeExplainer, interventional perturbation with a background sample of 2,000 alerts). Bakker (model owner); the fairness sections were reviewed by the AI Governance Office on 3 May 2027.

sections.heading: Global explainability
sections.text: Global SHAP importance on the out-of-time sample ranks the ten most important features as follows: threshold_exceedance_ratio (14.8% of mean absolute SHAP), prior_productive_alerts_24m (11.2%), crr_class (8.9%), cash_share_inflow_90d (7.4%), hrc_flow_share_90d (6.1%), counterparty_novelty_30d (5.6%), turnover_vs_expected_ratio (5.2%), account_age_months (4.7%), velocity_in_out_72h (4.4%) and sbi_industry_risk (3.9%); together they account for 72.2% of total importance. SHAP dependence plots for these ten features are presented in annex XAI-A and were reviewed with Financial Crime Compliance, which confirmed that the main drivers and their direction are consistent with business expectations, for example the steep increase of the score for cash shares above 60% and for money being forwarded within 72 hours. The importance ranking is stable: the Spearman rank correlation of the importance of the top 20 features between the test and out-of-time samples is 0.93.

sections.heading: Dependence and monotonicity
sections.text: Compliance with the monotone constraints and the plausibility of the learned relationships were verified with partial dependence and individual conditional expectation (ICE) plots on the test sample for all 46 features: the eight constrained features are monotone in every one of 1,000 sampled ICE curves, and none of the unconstrained features shows an implausible shape. The unconstrained feature account_age_months shows a U-shaped effect (higher scores for very new accounts, consistent with the money-mule typology, and for accounts older than 25 years with sudden activity), which Financial Crime Compliance considered plausible. The interaction between threshold_exceedance_ratio and scenario group, which explains most of the uplift over the logistic benchmark, is shown in two-way partial dependence plots in annex XAI-A.

sections.heading: Local explanations and reason codes
sections.text: For every scored alert the local SHAP values of all 46 features are computed at scoring time and stored in the scoring log together with the prediction, so that a local explanation is available for every prediction used in the handling of alerts. The alert screen in FCM-CM shows the analyst the three features with the highest positive contribution as ranked reason codes, each mapped to one of 38 standard statements that were drafted by FEC Analytics and reviewed by Transaction Monitoring Operations and Financial Crime Compliance, for example RC-07 Large share of incoming funds forwarded within three days. The standard statements are maintained in the versioned table reason_codes_v3.csv; a statement is changed only through change management and with the approval of Financial Crime Compliance.

sections.heading: Fidelity of explanations
sections.text: The fidelity of the explanation method was tested: the sum of the SHAP values and the expected value reproduces the raw model output (log-odds) for all 158,850 out-of-time alerts with a maximum absolute difference of 2×10⁻⁶, confirming additivity. Explanation stability was tested by perturbing 5,000 alerts with small changes (±1% on continuous features): the top reason code remained unchanged for 97.6% of alerts and the top three reason codes as a set for 93.1%. In a usability test with 18 analysts, the reason codes were rated as helpful for the investigation in 81% of 360 reviewed alerts; the four statements rated least clear were reworded.

sections.heading: Fairness methodology
sections.text: Fairness was tested before approval on the out-of-time sample for sex, age group (18–29, 30–44, 45–64, 65 and older) and nationality group (Dutch, other EEA, non-EEA), the protected characteristics for which data are lawfully available from customer due diligence; other protected characteristics are not available and are not collected for this purpose. No special categories of personal data are processed for fairness testing: the attributes used are held in the separate secure validation area, joined by token only for the analysis and not used by the model, as approved by the Privacy Office under PO-2027-014. The favourable outcome is defined as an alert not being placed in priority bands P1 or P2, and the true-positive rate as the share of productive alerts placed in bands P1 to P3. Metrics are computed for the whole model; results by segment are reported in annex XAI-B.

sections.heading: Fairness results
sections.text: The ratio of favourable-outcome rates between the least and most favoured group is 0.96 for sex, 0.84 for age group (18–29 compared with 45–64) and 0.88 for nationality group (non-EEA compared with Dutch), all at or above the threshold of 0.80. The difference in true-positive rates between groups is 1.9 percentage points for sex, 4.1 points for age group and 3.1 points for nationality group, within the limit of five points, and calibration by group shows no significant deviation for any group (maximum absolute difference between predicted and observed productive rate 0.7 points). The lower adverse-impact ratio for the youngest age group reflects the higher share of money-mule alerts among young customers, where the productive rate is also higher (13.1% compared with 9.2% for 45–64); the calibration by group confirms that the difference in scores corresponds to a difference in observed outcomes.

evidence.quote: The ratio of favourable-outcome rates between the least and most favoured group is 0.96 for sex, 0.84 for age group (18–29 compared with 45–64) and 0.88 for nationality group (non-EEA compared with Dutch), all at or above the threshold of 0.80.

The difference in true-positive rates between groups is 1.9 percentage points for sex, 4.1 points for age group and 3.1 points for nationality group, within the limit of five points, and calibration by group shows no significant deviation for any group (maximum absolute difference between predicted and observed productive rate 0.7 points).

sections.heading: Analysis and mitigation of fairness breaches
sections.text: The candidate model before mitigation showed an adverse-impact ratio of 0.78 for age group 18–29, a breach of the 0.80 threshold; the root cause analysis attributed it to the feature account_age_months interacting with feedback-loop bias in the labels of young customers, and the breach was mitigated by an interaction constraint that prevents account_age_months from interacting with the scenario group and by capping the account-age effect, after which the ratio rose to 0.84 at a Gini cost of 0.2 points. The retention of hrc_flow_share_90d, which acts as a partial proxy for nationality group, is justified by the legal requirement to monitor links with high-risk jurisdictions and was approved by the AI Governance Office (AIGO-2027-009); removing it would reduce the Gini by 1.1 points and the nationality adverse-impact ratio would improve only from 0.88 to 0.91. Fairness metrics will be monitored quarterly under the monitoring plan of the MDD, with the same thresholds as amber triggers.

sections.heading: Robustness and security
sections.text: Perturbation tests applying changes of ±5% and ±10% to all continuous inputs changed the priority band of 2.3% and 4.6% of alerts respectively, below the 5% amber level at ±5%, and the auto-closure status of 0.9% of alerts at ±5%. Behaviour for missing, out-of-range and extreme inputs was tested with 120 constructed alerts: missing values follow the documented default direction learned by LightGBM, out-of-range values are capped by the feature caps, and no input produced an error or a score outside [0, 1]. Adversarial tests simulated evasion by a customer splitting cash deposits (S02), spreading funnel payments over more days (S07) and routing payments via an intermediate account (S05); detection of the simulated patterns fell by 18% to 34% for the targeted scenarios, but the prioritisation layer ranked the remaining alerts of these customers higher because of the prior-alert and velocity features, and the results were shared with Information Security in assessment ISA-2027-031, which also covers data poisoning and model extraction risks.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The prioritisation layer is explainable at global and local level, produces stable and faithful reason codes, meets the fairness thresholds of AI-STD-700 §9.2 after mitigation and is robust to realistic perturbations. The remaining residual risks are the feedback-loop bias of the labels (limitation L-TM-01), which is mitigated by the random review sample, and the evasion risk, which is addressed by the combination of scenarios and by the annual tuning cycle. The report recommends quarterly fairness monitoring per segment and an annual repeat of the adversarial tests with the scenario tuning cycle.

documents.title: TM version 3.0 implementation and testing report

sections.heading: Scope and summary
sections.text: This report documents the implementation testing of MDL-15 version 3.0 in the TMX platform (scenario thresholds and new scenario S18) and in the model execution platform MEP (prioritisation layer and band assignment), performed between 6 April and 31 May 2027. Implementation testing, record-level reconciliation and user acceptance testing were completed without open defects affecting outputs; the parallel run covered two monthly production cycles, and the model will be used in production only after the MRC approval and completion of the third parallel-run month. Report version 1.0 of 4 June 2027; author J. Mulder (FEC Technology test lead); reviewer S. Jansen; approved by M. Bakker (model owner).

sections.heading: Implementation specification and components
sections.text: Implementation followed the implementation specification IS-TM-3.0 version 1.1 approved by the model owner on 2 April 2027, which defines the production source field and lineage of all 46 input variables and identifies the one difference between development and production data sources (streaming instead of daily batch extract for SEPA Instant data). Production code is held in repository fec-technology/tm-scoring-service (tag release-3.0.0) and the TMX configuration in fec-technology/tmx-config (tag tmx-cfg-2027.1); both are tagged and retrievable. The implemented components are: TMX parameter tables for 18 scenarios and three objective-indicator rules, the feature service reading from the curated FDH schema, the scoring service loading the model artefact lgbm_tm_v3.0.0.txt, the calibration and band assignment, and the alert enrichment interface to FCM-CM.

sections.text: Implementation testing was performed by the FEC Technology test team, which is independent of the authors of the production code and, as MDL-15 is Tier 1, of the model development team in FEC Analytics. sections.heading: Test execution and defects
sections.text: Testing covered all 1,250 specified test cases, the mapping of every input variable from source to feature, all transformations, the handling of missing, invalid and boundary values, the band boundaries, all auto-closure exclusion rules and outputs for every segment and scenario group. The test plan, cases, results and 14 defects are documented in the test management tool (project TM30); the four defects affecting model outputs (among them an incorrect rounding of the threshold exceedance ratio and a missing auto-closure exclusion for PEP-related customers) were resolved and retested before the parallel run started, and the remaining ten cosmetic defects were closed by 28 May 2027. Regression testing of the 15 unchanged scenarios confirmed identical alert generation to version 2.0 on one month of masked data.

sections.heading: Scenario re-implementation
sections.text: The scenario implementation in TMX was reconciled against an independent Python re-implementation by the test team of the changed scenarios S02, S06, S07, S11, S12 and S14 and of the new scenario S18 on masked data of January to March 2027. Alerts were identical for S06, S07, S11, S12, S14 and S18. For S02 the TMX configuration produced 3.4% fewer alerts than the re-implementation; the difference was attributed to deposits via the business deposit service being booked with a one-day value-date lag and was accepted by the test lead as explained. The re-implementation used the scenario specifications of annex MDD-A and the parameter values of IS-TM-3.0 as inputs; the parameter values in the TMX tables were not compared field by field in this test.

sections.heading: Record-level reconciliation of scores
sections.text: Production scores were reconciled at record level with the development code on identical input data for 60,000 alerts (at least 10,000 per segment, except CO-1 with all 3,900 available alerts from the RDS supplemented by 2,410 synthetic alerts). All scores agreed within the tolerance of 10⁻⁶ absolute difference (maximum difference 3.1×10⁻⁸) and the priority band, auto-closure status and top three reason codes were identical for all records. One difference outside tolerance was found in the first run (1,204 alerts with a score difference up to 0.004), traced to the use of a different pandas version in the feature service; after aligning the environment all differences were within tolerance and no unexplained differences remained.

sections.heading: Parallel run
sections.text: A parallel run was performed because version 3.0 is a materially changed Tier 1 model: from 12 April to 31 May 2027 the version 3.0 scenarios and prioritisation layer ran daily in the pre-production environment on production data alongside the version 2.3 production model, covering the full daily production cycle and the monthly reference dates of April and May 2027. The analysis of the results shows 3.7% more alerts generated (expected 3.6%), 21.1% of alerts in the auto-closure band (expected 21.4%), migration between the version 2.3 and version 3.0 priority orders with 38% of alerts changing band, and no operational issues other than an increase of the scoring run time from 11 to 19 minutes, which remains within the batch window. documents.title: TM data feed quality and reconciliation report 2026

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: This report presents the data quality of the transaction monitoring data feeds of MDL-15 over calendar year 2026, the monthly reconciliations with source systems and the currency of the customer due diligence data used in expected profiles. The report supports the data quality assessment of the RDS (EVD-15-RDS chapter 6) and the Bank's obligation to ensure that all relevant customer, service and transaction data are fully and accurately included in the transaction monitoring process before monitoring. Report version 1.0 of 12 February 2027; author N. de Boer (FEC Data Management); reviewer S. Jansen; approved by M. Bakker (model owner).

evidence.quote: The report supports the data quality assessment of the RDS (EVD-15-RDS chapter 6) and the Bank's obligation to ensure that all relevant customer, service and transaction data are fully and accurately included in the transaction monitoring process before monitoring.

sections.heading: Feeds and critical data elements
sections.text: Seven feeds are in scope: SEPA credit transfers and SEPA Instant (Payments Hub), direct debits (Payments Hub), international payments (SWIFT gateway), card transactions (Card Transaction Store), cash deposits and withdrawals (Cash Management System, including Geldmaat), customer and CDD data (KYC-One and Customer Master Data) and alert and case data (TMX platform and FCM-CM). The 58 critical data elements of MDL-15 and the data quality expectations for them (rules, thresholds and reconciliation tolerances) were agreed between the model owner and the four Data Owners in the data sharing agreement DSA-FEC-2025-03, updated on 15 January 2027.

evidence.quote: The 58 critical data elements of MDL-15 and the data quality expectations for them (rules, thresholds and reconciliation tolerances) were agreed between the model owner and the four Data Owners in the data sharing agreement DSA-FEC-2025-03, updated on 15 January 2027.

sections.heading: Monthly reconciliation with source systems
sections.text: Every feed is reconciled monthly with its source system on transaction counts and values; differences above 0.1% are investigated and reported to Financial Crime Compliance. In 2026 all 84 monthly reconciliations (seven feeds, twelve months) were within 0.1% on counts and values except the SWIFT feed in November 2026 (0.27% of messages missing after the ISO 20022 migration), which was investigated under incident INC-2026-2214, corrected by a reload of 11,380 messages and reported to Financial Crime Compliance on 9 December 2026. Transactions of the missing messages were re-run through the scenarios after the reload; 14 additional alerts were generated and handled.

sections.heading: Annual reconciliation of critical data elements

sections.text: Attribute-level completeness was at least 99.5% for all transaction-level critical data elements in every month of 2026. The accuracy of the CRR class used by the model was verified against the CRR engine of MDL-16 for all customers monthly, with no differences.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The data quality of the TM data feeds in 2026 was adequate: all reconciliation breaches were investigated and resolved, and the open deficiencies are treated as described in EVD-15-RDS section 6.2. The data used by MDL-15 are fit for the intended use of transaction monitoring and for the development of version 3.0, subject to the limitations L-TM-05 to L-TM-07 of the MDD. The main improvement actions for 2027 are the completion of the CDD remediation programme for SB-1 customers and the addition of the counterparty country to the SEPA Instant message processing.

evidence.quote: The data quality of the TM data feeds in 2026 was adequate: all reconciliation breaches were investigated and resolved, and the open deficiencies are treated as described in EVD-15-RDS section 6.2.

deficiencies.rationale: The increase of the S11 turnover-deviation threshold for segment SB-2 from 250% to 300% is supported by an ATL productive share of 1.8%, but the report also presents the reduction of the SB-2 alert backlog by around 380 alerts per month as a benefit. The documented rationale does not demonstrate that the increase is risk-based rather than driven by operational capacity, and does not assess the SIRA risk covered by the removed band.

mitigation.text: Document a risk-based rationale for the S11 SB-2 threshold increase (typologies in the removed band, residual SIRA risk and compensating scenarios), remove the capacity argument from the decision record and have the rationale re-approved by Financial Crime Compliance.

deficiencies.rationale: The report states that BTL events were reviewed blind in the regular alert queue. The FCM-CM audit trail examined by Model Validation shows that the 2,220 BTL events were loaded with alert type code BTL-2026, which is visible in the analysts' queue view; the escalation rate of BTL events handled by analysts who opened the type field was markedly lower. The review was therefore not blind, and the zero-productive conclusions for the bands of 13 scenarios and for the raised S11 and S12 thresholds are not reliable.

mitigation.text: Repeat the BTL review for the raised S11 (SB-2) and S12 thresholds and for a sample of the other bands with test events that are indistinguishable from production alerts, and amend the BTL procedure to mask the alert type.

deficiencies.rationale: The fairness analysis reports true-positive-rate differences only at model level (maximum 4.1 percentage points). Model Validation's recomputation per scenario group shows a difference of 7.2 percentage points between the non-EEA and Dutch nationality groups for the geography scenario group, above the five-point limit, which is not visible in the documentation.

mitigation.text: Extend the fairness analysis and the quarterly fairness monitoring to scenario groups and segments, analyse the root cause of the geography-group disparity and mitigate it or justify it with AI Governance Office approval.

deficiencies.rationale: For a materially changed Tier 1 model the parallel run must cover at least one full production cycle and three monthly reference dates; the documented parallel run covers only the April and May 2027 reference dates.

mitigation.text: Complete the June 2027 reference date of the parallel run, analyse the results and add them to the implementation and testing report before go-live.

deficiencies.rationale: Scenario population exclusions are quantified for the own-account transfer exclusion of S05 and S08 and the public-body payment exclusion of S07, but the transaction-code exclusions configured in the TMX platform for eleven other scenarios (for example internal bookings and fee reversals) are listed without their volume.

mitigation.text: Quantify the volume of every scenario exclusion in the scenario library (annex MDD-A) and reference the analysis in the RDS documentation.
